questions.title: I’ve applied before. When can I re-apply?
questions.text: We are generally happy to consider re-applications 6 months after the previous one. Principally, we do this so that there is sufficient time for an applicant to build up additional experience in that 6 months for us to re-assess.

questions.title: Can I request for a refund for a fee for an application or form?
questions.text:
Refund is generally not allowed. However, these exceptions may apply:
- You have made duplicate payment for a form.
- You have filed duplicate forms.
- You have submitted a form which cannot be processed
- The IPOS examiner has not started work on your request for a search and/or examination report for a patent application.
A refund request can be submitted via IPOS Digital Hub. Forms which have been processed are generally not refundable.
Submission of a request for refund does not guarantee a refund and is subject to approval. You are advised to check your forms carefully before submitting them.

questions.title: How do I apply to revoke a patent?
questions.text:
Any person may apply to revoke a patent for an invention on any of the grounds set out in Section 80 of the Patents Act.
The procedure on application for revocation, as set out in Rule 80 of the Patents Rules, commences with the filing of Patents Form 35 with a prescribed fee accompanied by a statement setting out fully the grounds of revocation including the facts on which the applicant relies and the relief which he seeks.

questions.title: How much does it cost to apply for a patent?
questions.text:
The two main costs involved in a patent application would be the official filing fees and your patent agent's fees (if you engage one).
The total cost varies from case to case depending on the approach you take and the complexity of the case. A list of the official fees can be found here.

questions.title: I have been asked by the Registrar to provide evidence of use of my trade mark by way of statutory declaration.
questions.text:
A statutory declaration is a declaration sworn before a Commissioner for Oaths or a Notary Public.
You may refer to "Chapter 6 - Evidence of Distinctiveness Acquired Through Use" of our Trade Marks Work Manual to help you prepare and present evidence of use of your trade mark.
You may refer to the sample statutory declaration to file evidence of use to file your evidence.

questions.title: What happens if the renewal fee is not paid on time?
questions.text: The renewal application can be lodged, at its earliest, 6 months before the design's renewal date is due. If you miss the renewal date, you can still lodge the renewal application within 6 months after the renewal date, but the prescribed late fee will apply. If you do not submit a renewal application within these dates, your design registration will lapse.

questions.title: How do I contact EMA?
questions.text: Please visit our website for EMA’s contact details.

questions.title: Can I get the HPV vaccination and any other vaccination at the same time?
questions.text:
If you have recently received the COVID-19 vaccine (e.g. in the last 14 days), you can still receive the HPV vaccine. An interval of at least 14 days before or after the COVID-19 vaccine is encouraged, but is not strictly necessary.
Please consult your doctor for the latest guidelines.

questions.title: Can MediSave be used for the co-payment after subsidy for vaccinations?
questions.text:
Those eligible for subsidised vaccination may also use their MediSave to cover the out-of-pocket expense at CHAS GP clinics and polyclinics.
Please check with your preferred clinic if the clinic is able to process the remaining co-payment via MediSave. If they do, please check with them on your eligibility to pay via MediSave.

questions.title: How should I take the HPV vaccine?
questions.text:
For females aged 9 – 14 years at the time of the first dose, a total of 2 doses are recommended. The second dose may be given 5 to 13 months after the first dose.
For females aged 15 years and above at the time of the first dose, a total of 3 doses are recommended. The second dose may be given between 1 to 2.5 months after the first dose, followed by the third dose between 5 to 12 months after the first dose.
If you have taken one type of HPV vaccine for the first dose and wish to change to the other type of HPV vaccine for the second dose, it is generally fine to do so. Please discuss with your doctor about your specific situation should you wish to change vaccine type for the second or third dose.

questions.title: If I do not have enough in my MediSave, and I am not able to pay the remaining co-payment, are there other ways to receive the vaccination?
questions.text:
At CHAS GP clinics, these nationally recommended vaccinations are fully subsidised for those who hold the Public Assistance card.
Patients who go to the polyclinics for their vaccination(s) and have financial difficulties in paying for their bills can approach the social worker at polyclinics to enquire for assistance.

questions.title: What are some common side-effects of the flu vaccine?
questions.text:
Some people may feel faint after the vaccination.
Sit for 15 minutes to avoid fainting.
Soreness, redness, or swelling at the injection site, slight headache, body aches or tiredness; fever of more than 38'C is not common.
- These side effects usually go away on its own within 2 to 3 days
- You may take Paracetamol to help to relieve the pain or fever

questions.title: What precautions should I follow before receiving the flu vaccine?
questions.text:
Inform your healthcare professional if:
- You are allergic to this vaccine or any of the other ingredients of this vaccine
- You have a history of Guillain-Barr Syndrome (a rare nerve condition)
- You are pregnant or breastfeeding

questions.title: What precautions should I follow before receiving the HPV vaccine?
questions.text:
Consult your doctor to find out if a vaccination is suitable for you if:
You are pregnant or planning to become pregnant
You are not feeling well and having a fever
You are allergic to this vaccine or any of the other ingredients of the HPV vaccine
You are taking any other medications

questions.title: What precautions should I follow before receiving the pneumococcal vaccine?
questions.text:
Inform your healthcare professional if:
You are allergic to this vaccine or any of the other ingredients of this vaccine
You have a history of Guillain-Barré syndrome (a rare nerve condition)
You are pregnant or breastfeeding

questions.title: Where can I find the full list of CHAS GPs that offer subsidised vaccinations?
questions.text:
The full list of CHAS GPs can be found (here) .
Before heading down, please call the clinic to check if they offer the specific vaccine you’re looking for, as vaccine availability may vary.
Enrolment on the Health Appointment System (HAS) is voluntary for clinics. However, you can still use HAS to book an appointment online at an available CHAS GP clinic without needing to call the clinic directly.

questions.title: Who should receive the HPV vaccination?
questions.text: In Singapore, according to the National Childhood Immunisation Schedule (NCIS) and National Adult Immunisation Schedule (NAIS), HPV vaccination is recommended for females aged 9 to 26 years.

questions.title: What are the infection prevention control measures to minimise transmission at home?
questions.text:
You may wish to observe the following guidelines while recovering at home to minimise risk of transmission:
1. Take appropriate infection prevention control measures during your recovery at home. Should you reside with a vulnerable household member, preventive measures such as wearing a mask and not sharing a room with other household members should be taken to mitigate infection spread. Alternatively, consider other accommodation arrangements, if possible.
2. Practise good personal hygiene by washing your hands regularly with soap and water.
3. You may wish to monitor your oxygen saturation using an oximeter and temperature if unwell.

questions.title: I was tested positive. Can I recover at home with other household members?
questions.text: Yes. You can recover at home with other household members who are well. Do take precautionary measures to minimise the risk of transmission.

questions.title: Why do I have to be quarantined?
questions.text: You are under quarantine as you were identified as a close contact of a mpox case. The prevailing definition of a “close contact” means that you were in close proximity to an mpox case during his/her infectious period for a significant period of time.

questions.title: Why do I have to be isolated?
questions.text: Isolation is necessary to limit the spread of the virus in the community.

questions.title: Are pets allowed at my home while I am under isolation order?
questions.text:
Pets are allowed to remain at home during your isolation period. However, as a precaution, you may wish to minimise direct contact with them as animals can be infected.
When possible, delegate pet care to other household members and keep pets away from personal items, beddings, and clothing, etc.
Good hygiene should be practised, including thorough handwashing after handling pets. Veterinary attention should be promptly sought for animals that are unwell.

questions.title: What is an MOH-designated Isolation Facility? Who is it managed by?
questions.text:
An MOH-designated Isolation Facility is a facility set up for persons under quarantine due to risk of exposure to infectious diseases of concern, including mpox.
Currently, there is one designated facility which is managed by a managing agent contracted by the Ministry of Health (MOH). If required, MOH can activate other isolation facilities located at various locations in Singapore.

questions.title: Where can I find the latest local updates on the mpox situation?
questions.text: For information on the local situation, please refer to CDA’s website: Weekly Infectious Diseases Bulletin 2025 | Communicable Diseases Agency

questions.title: What should I do if I suspect I might have been infected with mpox?
questions.text: You should see a doctor immediately and inform him/her of your recent exposure and/or travel history. Your doctor will assess your condition accordingly.

questions.title: What measures can I take to protect myself from mpox?
questions.text:
Members of the public are strongly advised to maintain vigilance and take the following precautions, where relevant:
Observe and practise good personal hygiene at all times.
Wash your hands regularly with soap, especially before handling food or eating, after going to the toilet, or when hands are dirty from coughing or sneezing. If water is not available, use an alcohol-based hand sanitiser that contains at least 60% alcohol.
Avoid contact with persons who are unwell (e.g., those with rash or other lesions).
Avoid sharing common items that may be contaminated with bodily fluids.
Practice safe sex, including avoiding high-risk sexual activities such as having multiple sex partners or engaging in casual sex.
When travelling, avoid feeding or touching animals, especially stray or wild animals, and the consumption of bush meat.
Travellers from countries affected by mpox should monitor for symptoms for 21 days upon their return from these countries. Please refer to CDA Health Advisory for Travellers for precautionary measures to be taken when travelling.
Seek medical attention immediately if you become unwell or develop symptoms such as sudden onset of high fever, swollen lymph nodes and rash, and inform the doctor of your travel or exposure history.

questions.title: What is mpox?
questions.text:
Mpox is a disease caused by the monkeypox virus (MPXV). The virus is part of the same family as the virus that causes smallpox. Mpox is not related to chickenpox.
Mpoxis endemic in parts of Central (Clade I) and West Africa (Clade II). It is a zoonotic disease, meaning it can spread from animals to humans. The virus has been found in animals including squirrels, Gambian poached rats, dormice, different species of monkeys and others.

questions.title: What is an Isolation Order (IO) or a Quarantine Order (QO)?
questions.text: An Isolation Order (IO) or a Quarantine Order (QO) is a legal order issued under the Infectious Diseases Act 1976. It may be issued to a person who is suspected or confirmed to be a case or an at-risk individual (e.g. exposed contacts) of an infectious disease. The IO or QO is necessary to limit the spread of the virus in the community.

questions.title: What if I refuse medical examination and/or to be isolated / quarantined?
questions.text:
A person who fails to comply with an Isolation Order (IO) or a Quarantine Order (QO) issued to him/her under the Infectious Diseases Act 1976, or who refuses to cooperate with Health Officers carrying out their duties under the Act, commits an offence and may be arrested without warrant.
The penalty for a first offence is a fine of not exceeding $10,000 or imprisonment for a term not exceeding 6 months or both. For a second or subsequent offence, the penalty is a fine not exceeding $20,000 or imprisonment for a term not exceeding 12 months or both.

questions.title: What do I do if I feel unwell while I am isolating at home?
questions.text:
You may contact MOH through the hotline number provided to you in your Isolation Order.
Should you experience the following: shortness of breath/breathlessness, chest pain or chest pressure, changes in your mental state, or any unusual symptoms with your nerves, headache or any neck stiffness, you should call 995 immediately for an ambulance. You are to inform the 995 operator that you are an mpox patient.

questions.title: What happens if I am unable to self-isolate at home?
questions.text: While self-isolation at home is the default option, we understand this may not be possible for everyone. If you cannot isolate at home, you will need to make alternative arrangements such as staying with relatives or friends who can provide a separate room.

questions.title: My doctor suspects I have mpox. What happens if I am tested positive?
questions.text: If confirmed positive for mpox, you will be isolated and managed clinically in a hospital setting or at home depending on the clinical assessment.

questions.title: My doctor suspects I have mpox. What happens if I am tested negative?
questions.text: If you are tested negative, you are not required to isolate.

questions.title: What happens during my recovery period?
questions.text: For those who qualify for recovery at home or at government isolation facility, you will receive regular telemedical consultations to assess your state of recovery. You may also be conveyed to NCID for additional reviews where necessary.

questions.title: My doctor suspects I have mpox. What happens after I have been tested?
questions.text: Depending on clinical assessment, you will either be isolated in a hospital setting or home.

questions.title: What are the symptoms of mpox?
questions.text:
Symptoms for mpox are indistinguishable across all clades and may include:
Skin rash often starting from the face before becoming generalised including involvement of palms and soles. However, presentation in the global outbreak of Clade II involves only a few or single localised lesions, especially in the genital and groin areas, which do not spread further.
Fever
Headache
Backache
Swollen lymph nodes
Muscle ache
General feeling of exhaustion or profound weakness
Symptoms usually appear within 21 days after being exposed to the virus. While asymptomatic and pre-symptomatic transmission are possible, a person is typically infectious from the onset of symptoms until the skin lesions have scabbed over.

questions.title: When does my quarantine end?
questions.text: Your quarantine period ends at 12 noon on the last date indicated in your Quarantine Order, or when you receive a Revocation Order, whichever is earlier.

questions.title: I received a call from CDA notifying me of contact tracing. How do I verify if this is not a scam call?
questions.text: To verify the authenticity of calls from CDA, call CDA Hotline 6461 5340 to verify the authenticity of the CDA number and full name of the caller.

questions.title: I have been in recent contact with someone who was issued a Quarantine Order (QO). What should I do?
questions.text:
Monitor your health and seek medical consultation should you be unwell; informing the doctor that you have been in contact with an individual that is serving quarantine.
Please refer to https://www.cda.gov.sg/public/diseases/mpox for more information.

questions.title: I have been informed by CDA that I was in close contact with a confirmed mpox (Clade I) case and need to be quarantined. What should I do?
questions.text: If you have been informed that you had close contact with a confirmed mpox case and will be placed on quarantine, please return to your place of residence immediately and isolate yourself from the rest of your household. MOH will contact you with further details and arrangements for your quarantine.

questions.title: If I am unemployed and on Quarantine Order (QO), who can I go to for social and financial assistance?
questions.text: Please contact MOH at the contact number listed in the Quarantine Order (QO) for assistance.

questions.title: If I am unemployed and on Isolation Order (IO), who can I go to for social and financial assistance?
questions.text: Please contact an MOH Officer at the helpline number furnished in your isolation order.

questions.title: How will my test result be made known to me?
questions.text: The attending physician and/or MOH will inform you of the test result, i.e., whether you are tested positive or negative for the virus.

questions.title: How will I know if I have recovered from mpox?
questions.text: You will be assessed by a doctor who will advise you on your condition and recovery.

questions.title: How long will it take for me to be conveyed to a quarantine facility?
questions.text:
You will typically be conveyed on the same day you are first informed by MOH of your quarantine status and duration.
Please self-isolate while waiting for quarantine instructions and conveyance from MOH.

questions.title: How long is the recovery period?
questions.text: Mpox patients usually recover within two to four weeks, although serious illness and complications may occur especially in vulnerable persons (e.g., young children, pregnant women or immunocompromised individuals).

questions.title: How long does it take for my test result to be available?
questions.text: It typically takes up to 24 hours for your test results. If retesting or additional testing is required, the process will take longer.

questions.title: How is mpox spread?
questions.text:
Mpox can spread through physical contact with infected individuals, skin lesions and body fluids, contaminated materials and environments, or exposure to respiratory secretions. The virus can also spread from animals to humans, e.g., through bite or scratch from an infected animal, bush meat preparation, or direct contact with the blood, body fluids, or skin or mucosal lesions of infected animals.
Please refer to CDA’s website https://www.cda.gov.sg/public/diseases/mpoxfor more information on mpox.

questions.title: If I am under Quarantine Order (QO), do I have to pay for medical assessment and quarantine for mpox?
questions.text: Costs related to medical assessment and quarantine for the mpox will be borne by the Government of Singapore.

questions.title: Does MOH/CDA publish an update to the list of countries affected by mpox?
questions.text: MOH/CDA does not maintain an updated list of countries affected by mpox. Please refer to WHO’s website for the latest update on the global situation for mpox.

questions.title: Can vaccination protect oneself against mpox entirely?
questions.text:
The MVA-BN (JYNNEOS) vaccine is estimated to provide over 80% protection against mpox, although current data remains limited in concluding the level and duration of protection conferred by vaccination.
Individuals are therefore advised to continue adhering to the recommended precautions against the disease, such as avoiding high-risk sexual activities and practising good personal hygiene.

questions.title: Can mpox be transmitted through food?
questions.text:
Food (other than bushmeat) has never been identified as being associated with human cases of mpox. Currently, there is also no evidence that food packaging is a likely route of transmission of the virus. As such, the risk of mpox transmission through food is low.
Nevertheless, it is important to always adopt good personal hygiene and food safety measures. Individuals preparing food should ensure frequent hand washing with soap and water when handling food, ensure food is cooked thoroughly at high temperatures above 75°C and frequently wash and sanitise both equipment and premises such as all food contact surfaces and touchpoints, including counter tops, utensils and condiment containers.
For more tips, refer to SFA’s website.

questions.title: Can I quarantine together with my family member(s) / travel companion(s)?
questions.text: For public health reasons, a Person-Under-Quarantine (PUQ) must be isolated in a separate room from anyone not under quarantine orders, including family members and travel companions.

questions.title: Can I get vaccinated against mpox in Singapore?
questions.text:
The MVA-BN (JYNNEOS), a third-generation smallpox vaccine, is currently available in Singapore as Post Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) for persons who have been identified to be close contacts of confirmed mpox cases.
In line with international recommendations, mass population-wide vaccination is currently not recommended as a preventive strategy for mpox, as the risk to the general public remains low with disease transmission predominantly via close physical or prolonged contact. Members of the public are advised to take the recommended precautionary measures such as avoiding high-risk sexual activities and practising good personal hygiene.

questions.title: I have been informed by MOH/CDA that I was in close contact with a confirmed mpox case. Where will I be quarantined?
questions.text: If you are required to quarantine for mpox, you will serve your quarantine at an MOH-designated Isolation Facility.

questions.title: At the end of the isolation / quarantine period, will transport be provided for me to return home?
questions.text: You will be required to arrange your own transport to your place of residence after completion of the isolation / quarantine period.

questions.title: Are meals provided at the MOH-designated Isolation Facility? I have specific dietary needs.
questions.text:
Yes, meals are provided at the MOH-designated Isolation Facility.
If you have specific dietary needs, please inform the MOH Duty Officer or the facility’s Duty Manager as soon as possible to facilitate the necessary arrangements. Where the facility is unable to cater to your specific dietary needs due to late requests, you may make alternative meal arrangements (e.g. contactless food delivery from family or friends, or delivery services) at your own expense.

questions.title: What should I do if my child becomes unwell?
questions.text:
Babies (less than three months old) with fever (38°C and above) should be referred to the Children's Emergency for clinical assessment and considered for admission.
If your child has mild ARI symptoms (e.g. fever, cough, sore throat), supportive care and symptom-relieving treatment, such as treatment with fever-reducing medications, staying well-hydrated, and getting enough rest, are usually enough to manage the acute symptoms of COVID-19.
Keep your child at home until their symptoms resolve, and avoid close contact with others, especially vulnerable persons. They may return to school/childcare once they are well.
Seek medical attention promptly if your child develops any of the following symptoms:
High fever
Rapid/difficulty breathing
Lethargy or not interacting when awake
Difficulty in feeding (unable to drink or breastfeed)
Blue lips or face
Signs of dehydration (reduced or no wet diapers/urine output)

questions.title: Should I test myself with an ART if I suspect that I have COVID-19?
questions.text:
ART testing is no longer routinely needed for healthy persons with acute respiratory infection (ARI) symptoms.
Nonetheless, ART kits remain commercially available. Individuals who choose to self-test should note that a negative result does not always mean you are not infected as your symptoms may be caused by other common viruses or bacteria.
Persons with mild ARI symptoms, including those infected with COVID-19, should stay at home until their symptoms resolve. If there is a need to go out while symptomatic, they should exercise social responsibility by minimising social interactions, wearing a mask, and avoiding crowded places or meeting medically vulnerable persons.
Medically vulnerable persons such as seniors and those with chronic medical conditions, as well as persons with severe, prolonged, or worsening symptoms, should see a doctor.

questions.title: I am a Pregnant patient. What should I do if I become unwell?
questions.text:
Pregnant women are at higher risk of severe illness from COVID-19.
You are advised to recover under the care of your doctors. Monitor yourself, and if you develop fever, cough or difficulty in breathing, or severe, prolonged or worsening ARI symptoms, you should seek medical attention early.
If your gestational age is 28 weeks or greater, you are advised to seek medical attention.

questions.title: I am a patient ≥ 60 years old. What should I do if I become unwell?
questions.text: Medically vulnerable persons (i.e. elderly persons aged 65 years and above and those with chronic medical conditions) are at greater risk of severe disease or complications when infected with COVID-19. If you develop ARI symptoms, or have severe, prolonged or worsening ARI symptoms, you should consult your doctor for medical management.

questions.title: What are the common symptoms of COVID-19?
questions.text:
The signs and symptoms of COVID-19 infection range from mild respiratory symptoms to severe illnesses such as pneumonia.
Symptoms may start as mild, and some people may progress to more severe symptoms.
Severity of symptoms may change with new COVID-19 variants and can vary depending on prior vaccination status and past COVID-19 infection.
Infection is mild in the majority of persons and up to one in three infected persons are asymptomatic.
Common symptoms of COVID-19 include:
Fever
Chills
Sore throat
Cough
Nasal congestion, runny nose
Headache
Loss of taste or smell
Fatigue
Muscle aches
Nausea or vomiting
Diarrhoea
In severe cases, COVID-19 can manifest as pneumonia with shortness of breath and chest pain. Severe cases should seek immediate medical attention.
Persons with pre-existing medical conditions are at higher risk when they have COVID-19 and are advised to seek medical care early if they are worried about their condition. These include but are not limited to those taking immunosuppressive medication; those with chronic heart, lung, liver or rheumatological problems; those with HIV, diabetes, cancer or dementia.

questions.title: Why is mask-wearing still required for higher-risk healthcare settings and residential care settings?
questions.text:
MOH has retained the practice of mask-wearing for higher-risk healthcare and community care settings, including inpatient wards, emergency departments and residential care facilities. These are settings where vulnerable persons, including the elderly and immunocompromised, may need to access services, and where the risk of infection is compounded by large crowds and prolonged close contact with others who might be infected.
Hence, to protect the vulnerable persons receiving care and the healthcare staff delivering care services at these premises, mask wearing will continue to be required at these settings.

questions.title: When should I wear a mask?
questions.text:
From 1 March 2024, MOH has stepped down the masking requirements at lower-risk healthcare settings. Mask-wearing will no longer be compulsory for patients, visitors and staff in outpatient settings, including polyclinics, General Practitioner clinics, specialist outpatient clinics, dialysis centres, Traditional Chinese Medicine clinics and dental clinics. However, mask-wearing in these settings is still strongly encouraged for medically vulnerable persons, seniors and persons with acute respiratory infection (ARI).
To protect medically vulnerable persons and seniors, mask-wearing will continue to be required for higher-risk healthcare settings, including inpatient wards, emergency departments and residential care facilities*.
Inpatients of hospitals and residents of residential care facilities are not required to wear a mask. Nevertheless, as good practice, we encourage residents and inpatients to wear a mask if they are unwell or develop ARI symptoms.
Besides healthcare, other authorities may also require mask-wearing. Private enterprises may also opt to maintain mask-wearing requirements as company policy for workplace health and safety or business continuity reasons.
As mask-wearing is an effective way to minimise the risk of infectious diseases, we encourage members of the public, especially the elderly and immunocompromised, to wear masks in crowded places, or when visiting or interacting with vulnerable persons. We strongly advise individuals who are unwell with symptoms of COVID-19 or other respiratory infections to wear a mask when they need to leave their home.
*Residential care settings include Nursing Homes, Psychiatric Rehabilitation Homes, Psychiatric Sheltered Home and Inpatient Hospice.

questions.title: When should I seek emergency help? What symptoms should I look out for?
questions.text:
If you experience any one of the following symptoms, please call 995 immediately:
· Shortness of breath or difficulty breathing.
· Chest pain or pressure on your chest.
· Palpitations (if your heart is beating very fast or pounding).
· New confusion
· Drowsiness or loss of consciousness (fainting)
· If you have an oximeter, and the SpO2 reading remains below 92% for multiple readings taken while you are at rest.

questions.title: What is the treatment for COVID-19?
questions.text:
COVID-19 is generally managed with supportive treatment, depending on the patient’s clinical condition and symptoms.
Treatment and drugs for COVID-19 are available for infected cases with severe disease or persons who are at high-risk of severe COVID-19.

questions.title: What is the COVID-19 General Advisory?
questions.text:
Persons with mild acute respiratory infections symptoms, including those infected with COVID-19, should stay at home until their symptoms resolve. If there is a need to go out while symptomatic, they should exercise social responsibility by minimising social interactions, wearing a mask, and avoiding crowded places or meeting medically vulnerable persons.
Medically vulnerable persons such as seniors and those with chronic medical conditions, as well as persons with severe, prolonged, or worsening symptoms, should see a doctor.

questions.title: I may have been exposed to COVID-19 but I have a COVID-19 vaccination appointment soon. Can I still go get the vaccination?
questions.text:
If you are well and asymptomatic, you may proceed with your COVID-19 vaccination appointment.
If you have any further concerns, you may check with the vaccine provider.

questions.title: I have received a call from MOH. How do I verify if that is true?
questions.text:
To verify the authenticity of calls from MOH, you may wish to:
1. Take down the MOH number and full name of the caller who dialled your number.
2. Call MOH General Line 6325 9220 to verify the authenticity of the above information.
3. Please note that at all times, MOH will not ask for your financial details. MOH will also not ask you to collect documents from MOH, unless your company has an existing business with MOH.

questions.title: How to spot a scam call?
questions.text:
1. Official callers will never request your personal or financial information over the phone.
2. Official callers will never send you a recorded message.
3. Official local calls will usually not have a “+” prefix - this is likely to be a spoofed call which you should not answer.
4. Only incoming international calls have the “+” sign prefix.
MOH is aware of calls falsely informing recipients that the caller is from MOH, requesting your personal or financial information over the phone. We urge recipients not to respond to such calls.
Be vigilant. Always be sure of the authenticity of instructions before offering any personal or financial information.
To verify the authenticity of calls from MOH, call MOH General Line 6325 9220 to verify the authenticity of the MOH number and full name of the caller.
If you suspect you have been scammed, contact the police at 1800 255 0000 or submit a report via www.police.gov.sg/iwitness

questions.title: How does COVID-19 spread?
questions.text: COVID-19 is primarily transmitted through inhalation of infectious respiratory particles when an infected person coughs or sneezes. It can also be transmitted via contact with contaminated surfaces such as when a person touches these contaminated surfaces and then touches their eyes, nose or mouth.

questions.title: Do I have to pay for the ART and consultation? How much does it cost?
questions.text:
From 1 Apr 2023, there will no longer be extra subsidies at polyclinics for the testing (ARTs and PCRs) and treatment of all respiratory infections.
Singaporeans will continue to enjoy prevailing subsidies under the Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS) at CHAS General Practitioner clinics. At polyclinics, prevailing polyclinic subsidies will apply.

questions.title: I am well but I had tested positive for COVID-19. What should I do?
questions.text:
While there are no legal requirements for COVID-19-positive individuals to isolate, you are strongly encouraged to exercise personal and social responsibility to reduce transmission risks. In particular, persons who test positive for COVID-19 should:
· Stay away from work, school, or public places until their symptoms have fully resolved. If there is a need to go out while symptomatic, they should minimise social interactions, wear a mask, avoid crowded places and meeting medically vulnerable persons such as seniors or immunocompromised patients.
· Practise good hygiene, such as frequent handwashing and covering their mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing.

questions.title: Is the RSV (Respiratory Synctial Virus) vaccine available in Singapore?
questions.text:
There are two types of RSV vaccines available locally. The RSV vaccines are approved for prevention of lower respiratory tract disease (LRTD) caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) for certain groups of people.
If you are keen to receive the vaccine, do consult your doctor who will be able to recommend the type of RSV vaccine which is suitable for you.

questions.title: How does tuberculosis (TB) Spread?
questions.text:
TB is typically spread through prolonged exposure (days to weeks, rather than minutes to hours) to an individual with active TB disease.
When a patient with active TB disease coughs, TB bacteria is released into the air and may be inhaled by those around – prolonged exposure can result in acquiring TB infection.
A person cannot get TB from sharing cups, eating utensils, and food. TB is also not spread through shaking someone’s hand, kissing, or touching bed linens or toilet seats.

questions.title: Do I need to be a Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS) cardholder to enjoy the Healthier SG Chronic Tier under Healthier SG from 2024?
questions.text:
You will need to be a CHAS/ Pioneer Generation (PG)/ Merdeka Generation (MG) cardholder and be enrolled with a Healthier SG GP clinic to be eligible for the Healthier SG Chronic Tier. In this tier, CHAS/PG/MG cardholders with high medication needs, can access subsidies for selected common chronic medications* at prices comparable to polyclinics. You or your household members can sign up at www.chas.sg.
Healthier SG benefits are available/ accessible at your enrolled Healthier SG Clinic.
*Additional subsides for Medication Assistance Fund (MAF) medications on the Healthier SG Medication List are available only for CHAS Blue and CHAS Orange cardholders (including PG/MG cardholders who also hold a CHAS Blue/Orange card).

questions.title: Why can't I find my Healthier SG clinic of choice? What do I do if my existing General Practitioner (GP) is not a Healthier SG clinic?
questions.text:
For Healthier SG, residents can enrol only with a clinic that is participating in Healthier SG. GP clinics that are not Healthier SG will not be available for selection.
As you will need to enrol with a Healthier SG GP clinic to access Healthier SG benefits, you are strongly encouraged to choose from the list of Healthier SG clinics in HealthHub.
You may continue to visit non-Healthier SG clinics even after your enrolment. However, Healthier SG benefits will not be applicable at clinics that you are not enrolled with, so you would only be able to enjoy the existing schemes such as CHAS and MediSave.
If your current GP is not on Healthier SG, you could also encourage your GP to onboard Healthier SG.

questions.title: Who do I contact should I need to amend my appointments for referrals?
questions.text: Please inform the clinic you were referred to that you would like to change your appointment. If you are unsure of the clinic you were referred to, please contact your enrolled Healthier SG GP clinic for clarification.

questions.title: What is the difference between this donation and Mosque Building and Mendaki Fund (MBMF)?
questions.text:
Mosque Building dan Mendaki Fund (MBMF) which is deducted from every Muslim employees’ monthly salary goes towards paying for the cost of constructing new mosque buildings and the upgrading of older mosques.
All operational costs, such as manpower and utility bills still depend large on donations from congregants. This portal aims fulfil that throughout online donations. All your donations will be channeled to the local mosques to meet their operational needs.

questions.title: Am I able to claim tax deductions on my donations to Ourmasjid.sg?
questions.text: Currently only donations to Institutions of a Public Character (IPCs) qualify for tax deductions. As mosques are not IPCs, the donations do not qualify for tax deductions.

questions.title: What are the benefits of paying my Zakat by Giro?
questions.text:
1. It is cashless and convenient.
2. You can better manage and plan for your long-term assets.

questions.title: Religious Guidance Regarding the COVID-19 Vaccination
questions.text:
The Muslim community is recommended to take the COVID-19 vaccination as it is a basic necessity to protect ourselves and also those around us. The past religious edicts of MUIS regarding medicine and vaccination have addressed the concerns regarding ingredients that are used.
Thus far, the production process of the COVID-19 vaccine and its ingredients are not in conflict with our past religious edicts. In fact, the processes that are involved to produce the COVID-19 vaccination are not against any principles and values of the Islamic Shariah.
OFFICE OF THE MUFTI, 13 DEC 2020

questions.title: How do I apply to increase my contribution to the Mosque Building and Mendaki Fund (MBMF)?
questions.text: You may fill up the 'Change Application' form available on https://www.muis.gov.sg/mosque/Mosque-Infrastructure/About-MBMF/Employer-Information and indicate clearly your revised contribution in the respective fields.

questions.title: How much is the current contribution rate to Mosque Building and Mendaki Fund (MBMF)?
questions.text:
You may visit the link below for the current contribution rate to MBMF:
https://www.muis.gov.sg/mosque/Mosque-Infrastructure/About-MBMF/Employer-Information

questions.title: Does a Muslim-owned eating establishment require Halal certification from Muis?
questions.text:
In general, halal certification is voluntary in Singapore. Owners of eating establishments, Muslims and non-Muslims alike, are advised to obtain MUIS Halal certification as this provides an independent testimony and assurance that the food they serve is halal.
However, we do not penalise Muslim-owned companies should they make halal claims about their operations, as it is their religious responsibility to ensure so.

questions.title: What is the maximum number of people in a group?
questions.text: A group can have a maximum of 10 applicants only.

questions.title: What if I do not have a Singpass account?
questions.text: You can register for a Singpass account on the Singpass website (https://www.singpass.gov.sg). Alternatively, you may visit a Singpass counter for assistance. You can locate the nearest Singpass counter at https://go.gov.sg/singpass-counters.

questions.title: Can I receive another (non-COVID-19) vaccine at the same time as COVID-19 vaccine? How long do I have to wait before getting other vaccines?
questions.text: The vaccines can be administered together with other non-COVID-19 vaccines across all ages.

questions.title: Where can I find out more about the COVID-19 vaccines?
questions.text: Learn more about COVID-19 vaccines by visiting the MOH website.

questions.title: What should I take note of on vaccination day?
questions.text:
Wear short sleeved or clothes where the sleeves can be rolled up.
Bring your ID (NRIC/FIN/Student Pass/Birth Certificate).
Male vaccinees aged 12 – 29 years who are receiving any dose of Moderna/Spikevax, Pfizer-BioNTech/Comirnaty or Novavax/Nuvaxovid COVID-19 vaccines should refrain from participating in strenuous physical activities for one week after vaccination.

questions.title: Where is the Healthier SG Enrolment Station nearest to me? How can I check if my GP / polyclinic is participating in Healthier SG?
questions.text: You may check for your nearest Healthier SG Enrolment Station and the list of participating clinics at https://gowhere.gov.sg/healthiersg . Simply enter your postal code or name of clinic to search.

questions.title: Can I get tested for COVID-19 at GP clinics?
questions.text:
Testing for COVID-19 is available at some GP clinics.
You are encouraged to contact the GP clinic before visiting. Your GP will ask about your symptoms and medical history and evaluate your condition.
If needed, your GP will administer the appropriate COVID-19 test at the clinic and these services are chargeable. If not, your GP may refer you to another location where swab testing is available. Self-testing with ART kits is also an option.

questions.title: What other charges should be included, aside from the rental fees, when stamping the tenancy agreement?
questions.text:
Apart from the contractual rent, you should include other considerations as stated in the lease/tenancy agreement, such as:
Advertising and Promotion charge
Furniture / Fittings charge
Maintenance charge
Service charge
Any other charges, excluding GST charges

questions.title: Should I include maintenance fees when stamping my tenancy agreement?
questions.text: The information stamped should be based on what is reflected in your tenancy agreement. If maintenance fees is one of the considerations stated in the agreement, it should be included as part of your contractual rent when stamping your document.

questions.title: Do I need to stamp again if there is a supplemental agreement due to an increase in rental fees?
questions.text: If there is an increase in rental, you are required to stamp the document under "Variation of Lease" and Stamp Duty is payable based on the difference in rent amount.

questions.title: My landlord had given me a supplemental document as the lease period has been amended to 10 months instead of the full year, am I required to stamp the changes?
questions.text: If there is a decrease in rental or the lease period is shortened, stamping of the document is not required as Stamp Duty is not payable. There will not be any refund of Lease Duty paid previously.

questions.title: The landlord terminated my lease earlier than the agreed lease period. Do I need to make changes to the stamping record so as to get a refund?
questions.text: No amendment is required if your lease is terminated early and there is no refund of Lease Duty paid previously in this circumstance.

questions.title: Do I need to stamp if I am only renting out a room to a friend or family member? There is no tenancy agreement, just verbal agreement.
questions.text:
Stamp Duty is a tax on document (physical or electronic).
If the tenancy agreement was executed via electronic modes such as WhatsApp, email, websites, or SMS, stamping is still required, and stamp duty is payable.
However, if the rental arrangement is through verbal agreement only, stamping is not required, and Stamp Duty is not payable.

questions.title: I'm a Singaporean, intending to jointly purchase a condo with my husband who is a US Citizen. This will be my 2nd residential property as I am an owner of a HDB. My husband does not own any residential property. How will the Additional Buyer’s Stamp Duty (ABSD) be computed on our joint purchase?
questions.text:
For purchases involving multiple buyers with different profiles, the higher applicable ABSD rate will be used.
As your spouse is a US Citizen, he will be eligible for the same Stamp Duty treatment as Singapore Citizens under the Free Trade Agreement ABSD Remission.
Given that this joint purchase will be your second residential property and you own an HDB, ABSD at the applicable rate will be imposed on the higher of the purchase price or market value.
topics: Stamp Duty / Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty (ABSD)

questions.title: Am I able to arrange for my Additional Buyer’s Stamp Duty (ABSD) to be deducted from my CPF account?
questions.text:
As Stamp Duty is payable within 14 days from the date of purchase, you will need to:
Pay Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty (ABSD) in cash first.
Subsequently obtain reimbursement from your CPF account.
Drawing upon CPF savings to pay Stamp Duty is under CPF's purview. For further clarification, please contact CPF Board.
topics: Stamp Duty / Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty (ABSD)

questions.title: If I am a US Citizen purchasing my first residential property in Singapore, will I incur Additional Buyer’s Stamp Duty (ABSD)?
questions.text:
For foreigners purchasing a property in Singapore, ABSD at the applicable rate will be payable.
Under the Free Trade Agreement ABSD Remission, as a US Citizen, you will receive the same Stamp Duty treatment as Singapore Citizens.
If this purchase is your first residential property, you will not incur ABSD. The ABSD rate for the purchase of subsequent residential properties will be based on the applicable rates for Singapore Citizens.
topics: Stamp Duty / Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty (ABSD)

questions.title: My wife and I are Singapore Citizen and we jointly own an apartment. We intend to jointly purchase a terrace house that is under construction. Do we need to pay Additional Buyer’s Stamp Duty (ABSD)?
questions.text:
ABSD is determined based on the buyer's profile and the number of residential properties owned at the time of purchase.
Since the terrace house will be your second residential property, you will need to pay ABSD at the applicable rate.
However, if you sell your apartment within 6 months from the date of TOP/CSC (whichever is earlier) of the terrace house, you might be eligible for an ABSD refund under the ABSD Remission for a Married Couple.
topics: Stamp Duty / Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty (ABSD)

questions.title: How can I pay the Buyer's Stamp Duty (BSD) using my CPF?
questions.text:
As Stamp Duty is payable within 14 days from the date of purchase, you will need to:
Pay Buyer's Stamp Duty (BSD) in cash first.
Subsequently obtain reimbursement from your CPF account.
Drawing upon CPF savings to pay Stamp Duty is under CPF's purview. For further clarification, please contact CPF Board.

questions.title: When must Stamp Duty be paid?
questions.text:
Stamp Duty must be paid within 14 days after signing a Contract or Agreement. If the document is signed overseas, payment is due within 30 days after its receipt in Singapore.
A document is only considered duly stamped when full payment is made. A penalty of up to 4 times of the duty payable may be imposed for late payment.
You may refer to IRAS website for the Parties Liable for stamp duty.

questions.title: What if I do not have enough funds to pay Stamp Duty, can Stamp Duty be deferred or paid by instalments?
questions.text: There are no instalment options available for Stamp Duty. Penalties will be imposed on late and non-payment of stamp duties.

questions.title: How do I compute the Stamp Duty payable?
questions.text: You may refer to the Stamp Duty Interactive Calculator for computation.

questions.title: How do I retrieve the stamp certificate after successful payment?
questions.text:
You may retrieve the current year and past 3 years' of Stamp Certificate(s) via the e-Stamping Portal.
Please refer to How do I Retrieve My Stamp Certificate for the detailed steps.

questions.title: What are the Stamp Duty payment modes available?
questions.text: You may refer to How to pay Stamp Duty for the payment modes available for Stamp Duty.

questions.title: I am a Singapore Citizen buying my first property. Do I need to pay Buyer's Stamp Duty (BSD)?
questions.text: Singapore Citizens are required to pay BSD as it is payable on all acquisitions of immovable properties in Singapore, regardless of the buyer's nationality or number of properties owned.

questions.title: I am buying a HDB shop with living quarters. Is my purchase subject to Buyer's Stamp Duty (BSD) rates for non-residential property?
questions.text: BSD rates for the residential and non-residential components would be applied respectively based on the value attributable for each component.

questions.title: I am buying a semi-detached house with land zoned “Residential”. The semi-detached house has been approved as a childcare centre. Is my purchase subject to Buyer's Stamp Duty (BSD) rates for non-residential property?
questions.text: For the acquistion of the subject property, the applicable BSD rates would depend on the zoning of the land. Since the land is zoned “Residential”, BSD rates for residential property applies.

questions.title: I am buying a land zoned “Commercial & Residential”. What is the market value attributable to the residential and non-residential component?
questions.text:
For a land zoned “Commercial & Residential”, 60% Gross Floor Area (GFA) of the land is deemed attributable for residential purpose and the remainder for non-residential purpose.
You may get a professional valuer to value the part of the property attributable to residential and non-residential purposes.

questions.title: I am a Singapore Citizen currently owning only one private apartment. I am considering selling it and buying a terrace house. Do I have to pay Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty (ABSD) when I buy the terrace house?
questions.text:
ABSD is determined based on the buyer's profile and the number of residential properties owned at the time of purchase.
As a Singapore Citizen, if you have already signed the contract to sell your current private apartment before accepting the Option to Purchase for the terrace house, you will not need to pay ABSD.
However, if you have not signed the contract for the sale of your private apartment prior to accepting the Option to Purchase for the terrace house, your purchase of the terrace house will be considered your second residential property. In this case, you will be required to pay ABSD at the applicable rate.
topics: Stamp Duty / Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty (ABSD)

questions.title: I am a Singapore Citizen currently owning a private flat. If I were to downgrade to an HDB resale flat, do I have to pay Additional Buyer’s Stamp Duty (ABSD) on the HDB resale flat?
questions.text: As HDB’s rules require buyers to dispose of their private properties within 6 months of the resale flat purchase, ABSD remission will be given upfront to purchasers of HDB flats. Hence you would not need to pay ABSD when you purchase the flat.
topics: Stamp Duty / Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty (ABSD)

questions.title: My wife and I are SC and we jointly own an apartment. We intend to jointly purchase a terrace house that is under construction. Do we need to pay Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty (ABSD)?
questions.text: The ABSD of 17% is payable as the terrace house will be your second property. However, if you dispose of your apartment within 6 months from the date of TOP/CSC (whichever is earlier) of the terrace house, you may be eligible for the refund of ABSD.
topics: Stamp Duty / Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty (ABSD)

questions.title: I am a Singapore Citizen currently owning a 20% share in a house co-owned with my mum. Should my mum transfer her 80% share of the house to me, do I need to pay ABSD? If I were to buy another private flat after that, what would be the Additional Buyer’s Stamp Duty (ABSD) rate?
questions.text:
As you are a Singapore citizen and currently own just one residential property, there will not be any ABSD payable when you acquire additional ownership in the same property from your co-owner, your mother.
However, please take note that BSD will still apply to the acquisition of your mother’s 80% share of the property.
Should you decide to purchase another private flat after acquiring your mother's share, the purchase of the private flat will be your second property and you will be subject to ABSD at the applicable rate.
topics: Stamp Duty / Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty (ABSD)

questions.title: I am a Singapore Citizen married to an Singapore Permanent Resident. Both of us do not own any property in Singapore. If we jointly purchase our first matrimonial home, do we need to pay Additional Buyer’s Stamp Duty (ABSD)?
questions.text:
A married couple with at least one Singapore Citizen spouse, jointly purchasing a residential property and both the spouses do not own any residential property at the time of purchase, may be eligible for upfront ABSD remission; refer to ABSD Remission for a Married Couple.
If all conditions are met, ABSD will not be payable on the purchase of the 1st matrimonial property.
topics: Stamp Duty / Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty (ABSD)

questions.title: I am a Singapore Citizen married to a Singapore Permanent Resident. We jointly own a private apartment. If we buy another completed house jointly, what is the Additional Buyer’s Stamp Duty (ABSD) payable by us?
questions.text:
For purchases involving two or more buyers with different profiles, the higher applicable ABSD rate will apply.
If your spouse is a Singapore Permanent Resident or a foreigner and the joint purchase of the new house is your second residential property, you will be required to pay ABSD at the applicable rate on the higher of the purchase price or market value.
In the event that you sell/dispose of your private apartment within 6 months from the date of purchasing the new house, you might qualify for an ABSD refund under the ABSD Remission for a Married Couple.
topics: Stamp Duty / Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty (ABSD)

questions.title: If I am in the process of obtaining Singapore Citizenship or Singapore Permanent Resident at the time of purchasing a property, can I qualify for a lower ABSD rate or apply for a refund later, based on my new residency status?
questions.text:
The ABSD payable amount is based on the profile of the purchaser and the count of residential properties owned as at the date of purchase.
You must have been granted the Singapore Citizen or Singapore Permanent Resident status by the Immigration and Checkpoint Authority (ICA) as at the date of property purchase to enjoy lower ABSD liability. The date of issue reflected in the IC collection slip would be taken as when the status was granted.
topics: Stamp Duty / Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty (ABSD)

questions.title: When do I need to pay Seller's Stamp Duty (SSD) and can the payment be deferred?
questions.text:
SSD must be paid within 14 days after the date of the executed sale contract, otherwise, a penalty will be imposed for late stamping and payment. There is no deferment for Stamp Duty payment.
However, for properties undergoing collective sale, requests may be considered favorably for the waiver of the penalty incurred up to the later of the following dates, whichever is applicable:
(1) Date that the Strata Titles Board grants the Collective Sale Order;
(2) 30 days from the date of decision made by the High Court with no further objection; or
(3) Date of decision made by the Court of Appeal.
Such requests are subject to the following conditions:
(1) The collective sale contract is stamped and
(2) The waiver request is submitted to the Commissioner of Stamp Duties where both conditions are fulfilled within 14 days from the date of the executed contract.
To submit the request for waiver, please perform the following steps:
(1) Log on to e-Stamping Portal
(2) Select ""Requests""
(3) Select ""Apply for Assessment/ Appeal""
(5) Select ""Appeal"" under New Application.
Please be informed that requests to waive penalties incurred up to the date that the collective sale is legally completed or the date that you receive the sale proceeds will not be acceded to.

questions.title: My wife and I purchased a private residential property on 1 Oct 2005. On 10 Mar 2022, my wife transferred her half share of the property to me by way of gift. As a result, I became the sole owner of the property. I sold the property on 1 Sep 2022. As I have been an owner and occupant of the property since 1 Oct 2005, do I need to pay Seller's Stamp Duty (SSD) on the sale?
questions.text:
Since you acquired your wife's half share of a property on 10 Mar 2022 and sold the property on 1 Sep 2022, which is within the SSD holding period, SSD at the applicable rate is payable on the half share of the property that you acquired from your wife.
SSD payable amount is computed based on the higher of the selling price or market value of the property.

questions.title: I purchased (i.e. signed the Agreement for Lease) a replacement flat under the Selective En-bloc Redevelopment Singapore Citizen Scheme (SERS) on 1 Feb 2021. On 1 Sep 2023, HDB confirmed that I have fulfilled the Minimum Occupation Period (MOP) of 7 years for the replacement flat and granted approval for me to sell the replacement flat. I sold my replacement flat on 1 Oct 2023. Will the sale be subject to Seller's Stamp Duty (SSD)?
questions.text:
Since you are selling a replacement flat acquired under the Selective En-bloc Redevelopment Singapore Citizen Scheme (SERS) on 1 Oct 2023, within the SSD holding period, you will still be subject to SSD at the applicable rate, despite fulfilling the Minimum Occupation Period (MOP) of 7 years.
The payable SSD amount is calculated based on the higher of the property's selling price or its market value.

questions.title: I was not adjudged a bankrupt when I sold my private residential property. However, I was adjudged a bankrupt shortly after I sold my property. Can I qualify for Seller's Stamp Duty (SSD) exemption and seek a refund of the SSD paid on the sale?
questions.text:
If you were not adjudged a bankrupt at the time of selling your private residential property, you would not qualify for the SSD exemption given to an adjudged bankrupt who has to dispose of the property as a result of bankruptcy.
Therefore, you would not be able to seek a refund of the SSD paid on the sale.

questions.title: I am disposing of an HDB shop with living quarters within the holding period. Do I need to pay Seller's Stamp Duty (SSD)?
questions.text: For disposal of HDB shop with living quarters, SSD is payable on the value of the part permitted for residential use if the property is disposed of within the holding period.

questions.title: How do I stamp my tenancy agreement?
questions.text: Please stamp your tenancy agreement using the e-Stamping Portal. You may refer to the detailed guide on How to stamp Lease or Tenancy Agreements.

questions.title: How do I calculate the Stamp Duty payable for Lease /Tenancy Agreement?
questions.text:
Stamp Duty is calculated using Lease Duty rates and is based on the higher of the contractual rent or the market rent.
Average Annual Rent (AAR) is determined based on the higher of the average annual contractual or annualized market rent, including other considerations.
Properties with an AAR of $1,000 or less are exempt from Stamp Duty.
For properties with an AAR exceeding $1,000, please refer to the applicable Lease Duty rate.
You may use the Stamp Duty Calculator to estimate your lease duty.

questions.title: Do I need to pay Stamp Duty for a novation agreement where all the terms and conditions remain the same except for a new tenant?
questions.text:
If there is no change in the rent and lease period nor any premium or consideration paid for the novation of lease under the Novation Agreement, there is no Stamp Duty payable.
However, if there is any consideration paid under the Novation Agreement, Stamp Duty is payable and is computed on the consideration based on conveyance (BSD) rates.

questions.title: I paid Stamp Duty on a Lease/Tenancy Agreement, but the Lease/Tenancy Agreement is terminated/aborted. Can I seek a refund of Stamp Duty?
questions.text:
Refunds may be allowed on rescinded or cancelled documents which have not been ""made use of"" if all the conditions are met under the Terminated Lease Remission.
Application for refund under this remission has to be made within 6 months from the date of termination. If approved, Lease Duty in excess of $50 will be refunded to the party liable, i.e. the tenant/lessee.

questions.title: How can I get more information about the CDC Vouchers Scheme?
questions.text: Please visit the CDC website https://vouchers.cdc.gov.sg
topics: CDC Vouchers (Merchants) / About CDC Vouchers Scheme

questions.title: What do I do if I do not have a Singpass?
questions.text: Please visit https://www.Singpass.gov.sg to register for a Singpass account.

questions.title: If my next-of-kin passes away outside Singapore, should I report the death in the foreign country or in Singapore?
questions.text:
For deaths that happened overseas, the deceased's next-of-kin should register the death and obtain a death certificate from the foreign authorities in the country where the person had passed on. After that, you may report the death to ICA with the foreign death certificate.
Please refer to ICA website for more information on Reporting a Death that Occurred Overseas.

questions.title: How can the next-of-kin submit the digital death certificate to banks if they are requesting an "original" hardcopy?
questions.text:
For deaths that occur after 29 May 2022, only digital death certificates will be issued.
If the bank requests for an original hardcopy, you can provide the digital death certificate to the banks. The bank is able to verify these death certificates by scanning the QR code printed at the bottom right of the digital death certificates or via this link.

questions.title: Is it possible to issue the death certificate in another language?
questions.text:
All death certificates issued by ICA are in English. ICA does not issue death certificates in any other languages.
You may wish to have the document translated by a translator/agency recognised by the relevant foreign authorities for which this translation is required.
You are advised to check directly with the party requesting this translated death certificate on their requirements.

questions.title: How do I register the death of my next-of-kin after receiving a court order on their presumption of death?
questions.text: You may report the presumption of death to ICA online here.

questions.title: How long does it take for trusted persons to be notified when the deceased has passed away?
questions.text:
A Trusted Person will not be notified of the deceased's status.
Once the death has been reported to ICA, the Trusted Person(s) would be able to view the document(s) in their My Legacy dashboard, by logging in using their Singpass (if the user has selected the option for the Trusted Person(s) to view the document(s) after his/her death).

questions.title: What will happen to the joint property if one of the owner(s) passed away?
questions.text:
If the property is under joint tenancy, the person's share in the flat will be transferred to the remaining owner(s) and the remaining owners should lodge a Notice of Death (NOD) with Singapore Land Authority (SLA).
For HDB, the owner(s) can retain the existing flat provided that they:
are a Singapore Citizen (SC) or Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR)
are at least 21 years old; and
satisfy HDB's eligibility rules and conditions to own a flat.
You can refer to the following page on HDB under the title "Demise of joint owner" for more information.

questions.title: Is it possible for me to leave my HDB flat to a non next-of-kin?
questions.text:
You may wish to consider writing a will to ensure that the ownership of the HDB flat is distributed according to your wishes. In the absence of a will, your flat and other assets will be distributed in accordance with the Intestate Succession Act (ISA).
However, you should pay special attention to the ownership type of the HDB. If the flat is under joint ownership, the deceased shares will transfer to the remaining joint owners and cannot be willed away. Only HDB's that are solely owned, or owned via tenancy-in-common, can will away their share of the property according to their wishes. It is strongly advised that a lawyer is consulted for matters relating to writing your will.
You may read more information about retaining a flat following life events at HDB's website.

questions.title: How do I proceed to settle the inheritance / estate after the death of someone?
questions.text:
If the deceased had left a will, the named executor should apply for a grant of probate to execute his/her wishes in accordance to the will. If the will is accompanied by a schedule of assets, that provides a reference on the assets that need to be managed and distributed. Otherwise, the executor may need to contact organisations directly to check whether the deceased had assets, liabilities or accounts with them.
If the deceased did not leave a will, their next-of-kin may apply for a grant of letters of administration. Similarly, the next-of-kin may need to contact organisations directly to check whether the deceased had assets, liabilities or accounts with them should the NOK be unsure of the details of the deceased's estate.
You may refer to this page on My Legacy for more information.

questions.title: Can I create a new will using My Legacy vault?
questions.text:
The Vault in My Legacy provides a secure storage space for members of the public to upload official documents to share with their loved ones. The My Legacy website also provides information on will-writing.
However, My Legacy Vault does not provide will-writing services or a will template.
If you require in-depth information or guidance, you may wish to consider seeking independent legal advice. Wills are private legal instruments, and it is best to engage a lawyer to help you in drafting a will. Lawyers – particularly those specialising in wills and probate matters – are trained in the law relating to wills. They are therefore best placed to ensure a person’s will is drafted to accurately reflect that person’s wishes for how her estate is to be distributed after her death.
You may refer to the Ministry of Law’s website for a list of lawyers or law practices in Singapore. In particular, you may click on “Advanced Search” and select “Wills, Probate and Administration of Estate” under “Practice Area(s)”, before clicking “Search” to view the list of lawyers or law practices that practise that area of law. The Law Society of Singapore also provides a list of lawyers specialising in wills and probate matters.
You may also refer to go.gov.sg/legal-asst for other avenues that offer legal help.

questions.title: Where can I view my registered Lasting Power of Attorney?
questions.text:
After your LPA has been registered, you and your Donees can retrieve it at any time by logging in to the Office of the Public Guardian Online (OPGO) with your Singpass.
If you would like to keep a printed copy of the LPA for personal reference, you can print the PDF after downloading it from OPGO. However, the printed copy will be watermarked and cannot be used for transactions.
Please follow the steps below to view the full LPA:
Open the LPA with Adobe Acrobat Reader DC.
Click on the paper clip icon located on the left panel. This opens up a tab called ‘Attachments’.
Double click the attachment named LPA Form_Certified_XXXXX.pdf to view your full LPA.
Please ensure that your device’s default setting is opening the PDF via Adobe instead of web browser.
If you are unable to view your LPA on OPGO, please contact the Office of Public Guardian.

questions.title: How do I make changes to my registered Lasting Power of Attorney (LPA)?
questions.text:
To make changes to your registered Lasting Power of Attorney (LPA), including changing or adding a Donee, you will need to revoke your existing LPA and make a new one.
Before revoking your LPA, you must inform all your Donees in writing about your decision. You can notify them either by:
delivering a written notice in person
post
email
To revoke your existing LPA, log in to Office of the Public Guardian Online (OPGO) using your Singpass, to submit your notice of revocation.
Select Revoke LPA under your registered LPA.
Review and acknowledge the information provided.
Complete the required declarations.
Make payment.
Submit your notice of revocation.
If you are unable to access OPGO, submit your completed hardcopy revocation form to the Office of the Public Guardian by post, or via FormSG at https://go.gov.sg/opg-enquiry.
The Public Guardian may require you to provide further information or documents before revoking your registered LPA.
You may start drafting a new LPA while waiting for the cancellation of your existing LPA. However, the new LPA will only be accepted by OPG for registration after your existing LPA is cancelled. ( to adhere to copy in link)
Before submitting your new LPA for registration, you will need to have it certified by a Certificate Issuer.

questions.title: Is my Lasting Power of Attorney (LPA) still effective after I die?
questions.text:
An LPA is meant to cover situations when a Donor is still alive but lacks the mental capacity to make decisions. It is then when a Donee, who had been granted powers by the Donor prior to the lost of mental capacity through a legally valid LPA, is able to act on their behalf.
Once a Donor passes on, the LPA ceases to be effective.

questions.title: What is Advance Care Planning (ACP)?
questions.text:
ACP is an ongoing process of planning and preparing for your future health and personal care. It includes conversations about your:
personal beliefs
values
healthcare preferences
These will be shared with your loved ones and healthcare team. You may read more about ACP here.
The myACP service on My Legacy can only be completed if you:
have a Singpass account
are at least 21 years old
do not have any existing serious illness (e.g. Cancer, Chronic neurological diseases, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) and End-stage Lung Disease, Dementia, End-Stage Renal Failure (ESRF), Heart Failure, Severe Liver Disease)
do not have a Preferred Plan of Care (PPC) ACP or Disease Specific (DS) ACP
Otherwise, you may wish to contact your current healthcare team or an ACP facilitator directly for a discussion.

questions.title: How do I obtain more information on my deceased next-of-kin's bank accounts?
questions.text:
To obtain more information on a deceased's bank accounts, the next-of-kin would have to contact the bank(s) directly and explain that your loved one has passed on and you would like to check if they held an account with the bank. Do note that each bank may have its own processes with regard to disclosure of this information.
Unclaimed monies in bank accounts will continue to be held by the banks even when the accounts are inactive or if the account holder has passed on. As the banks are required to comply with customer information confidentiality requirements under the Banking Act, the banks are unable to disclose details pertaining to the bank account(s) held by the deceased without the appropriate court documents such as the Grant of Probate (if the deceased made a will) or Grant of Letters of Administration (if the deceased did not make a will).
You may check the Family Justice Courts website or enquire with the Family Justice Courts for more information on applying for these court documents.

questions.title: Will I be able to access the bank statements of my deceased next-of-kin?
questions.text:
As the banks are required to comply with customer information confidentiality requirements under the Banking Act, the banks are unable to disclose details pertaining to the bank account(s) held by the deceased without the appropriate court documents such as the Grant of Probate (if the deceased made a will) or Grant of Letters of Administration (if the deceased did not make a will).
You can check the Family Justice Courts website - https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/family/apply-for-letters-of-administration) or enquire with the Family Justice Courts for more information on the court procedure.

questions.title: How do I check whether my deceased next-of-kin made a CPF nomination?
questions.text: Please refer to this FAQ by the Central Provident Fund Board for more information on CPFB processes with regards to CPF Nomination.

questions.title: How do I pulverize the cremated remains of my deceased next-of-kin?
questions.text:
The National Environment Agency can only pulverised the cremated remains under the following circumstances:
a) At the time of collecting the cremated remains after cremation at Mandai Crematorium;
b) At the time of collecting the cremated exhumed remains after exhumation at Choa Chu Kang cemetery; and
c) For the usage of Inland Ash Scattering (IAS) Facility at Garden of Peace.

questions.title: What is the process for repatriating a body from Singapore, and is the export status indicated on the death certificate?
questions.text: The death certificate will only reflect details of the deceased and cause of death. To export a body out of Singapore, you will need to apply for an export permit with NEA Port Health. For more details, please visit NEA's website.

questions.title: Can non next-of-kins (e.g. social service practitioners, godchildren, funeral directors) download the digital death certificate for a deceased person with no next-of-kin (e.g. single elderly)?
questions.text:
Only Next-of-Kin of the deceased or persons authorised by the Next-of-Kin are allowed to download a copy of the digital death certificate from My Legacy.
The Next-of-Kin for this purpose are:
spouse,
parent,
child,
sibling,
grandparent,
grandchild,
aunt/uncle; and
niece/nephew.
For deceased with no immediate Next-of-Kin, individuals who are assisting in the post-death matters can approach the hospital or certifying doctor for a hardcopy printout of the death certificate.

questions.title: Do we still need to return the deceased's NRIC to the police?
questions.text: There is no longer a need to surrender the deceased’s NRIC in police station for physical invalidation. To prevent it from being misused, you can either destroy the NRIC or punch a hole in it.

questions.title: I need assistance in will-writing. Are there any avenues for help?
questions.text:
You may read up for more information at Write a will - MyLegacy@LifeSG.
If you require in-depth information or guidance, you may wish to consider seeking independent legal advice. Wills are private legal instruments, and it is best to engage a lawyer to help you in drafting a will. Lawyers – particularly those specialising in wills and probate matters – are trained in the law relating to wills. They are therefore best placed to ensure a person’s will is drafted to accurately reflect that person’s wishes for how her estate is to be distributed after her death.
You may refer to the Ministry of Law’s website for a list of lawyers or law practices in Singapore. In particular, you may click on “Advanced Search” and select “Wills, Probate and Administration of Estate” under “Practice Area(s)”, before clicking “Search” to view the list of lawyers or law practices that practise that area of law. The Law Society of Singapore also provides a list of lawyers specialising in wills and probate matters.
You may also refer to go.gov.sg/legal-asst for other avenues that offer legal help.

questions.title: Is there any legal requirement to make a will?
questions.text:
While there is no legal requirement to make a will, if you pass away without a will in Singapore, your assets will be distributed in accordance with the Intestate Succession Act. This means that the assets will be divided among the surviving family members according to a predetermined legal formula, which may not necessarily align with your specific wishes.
As such, it is highly advisable for you to create a will to ensure that your assets are distributed according to your wishes after your passing. Making a will also means you can name someone to legally manage your estate after your demise and carry out your wishes, especially if you do not have any next-of-kin.
You can read more about will-writing on the My Legacy website.

questions.title: Am I able to store my digital written will into this vault?
questions.text:
You can store a digital copy of your Will in My Legacy Vault by uploading the file under “Important Documents”, but this would not render the will as legally valid. As of today, for your Will to be generally recognised as legally valid, you must make sure that your will is printed or handwritten on a paper document and sign it in-person at the foot of the will.
With the given condition, only original copies of the Will would generally be accepted as legally valid by the Courts. For instance, the Family Justice Courts would require “the original will of the deceased” to apply for a Grant of Probate.
On My Legacy Vault, you can store information of where your original Will is located and share it with your Trusted Person(s).
Alternatively, you can also choose to do the same under Singapore Academy of Law’s (SAL) Wills Registry where they keep a record of where your Will is stored. You may wish to note that there are fees chargeable by SAL for depositing or searching for a record of the Will.

questions.title: If someone has only made an LPA and not a will, after they pass on, what will happen to their assets if there is no immediate family members to inherit it. Can their Donee act of their behalf?
questions.text:
An LPA only covers situations when a Donor loses mental capacity but is still alive and becomes invalid once the Donor passes on.
LPA Donee(s) can only make decisions based on the powers granted by the Donor when the Donor loses mental capacity up until the point of death.
