questions.title: What do I need to update if our law practice has a change of Managing Partner/Director?
questions.text:
If there is a change of Managing Partner/Director,
For Singapore law practices entities:
Please file a 'Notice of Change of Particulars' via eLitigation system on the appointments of the Singapore solicitors.
Thereafter, please update your licence particulars (the Managing Partner/Director section and the substantive appointments of the previous and new Managing Partners/Directors in the Lawyers section) via LSRA e-Services.
For foreign law practice entities:
If the new Managing Partner/Director does not have a Certificate of Registration ("CoR"), the law practice should apply via LSRA e-Services for a CoR for him/her, and indicate in the application form that the Registrant is the Managing Partner/Director.
If the new Managing Partner/Director has an existing CoR, the law practice should apply to update the CoR of the new Managing Partner/Director, indicating in the application form that the Registrant is the Managing Partner/Director, and updating his/her substantive appointment and job title.
The law practice should concurrently apply to update the CoR of the previous Managing Partner/Director on his/her substantive appointment and job title, or terminate the CoR, as applicable.
If and when the updates to the CoRs are approved, the law practice's licence record (the Managing Partner/Director section) will be automatically updated.
topics: Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals
Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals / Law Practice Entities

questions.title: How do we apply for approval to change the name of our law practice?
questions.text:
To seek approval to change the name of your law practice, please submit an update application via LSRA e-Services. In the Update application form, enter the new proposed name of the law practice and upload any relevant supporting documents, including the reasons for the name change, and submit the application.
If and when the application is approved, please update the Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority (ACRA) on the new name of your law practice and submit the updated ACRA business profile via Contact Us @OneMinlaw. Thereafter, your law practice's licence will be reissued (with a fee of $50) and its updated particulars will be transmitted to the Supreme Court's eLitigation system after 1-2 working days.
topics: Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals
Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals / Law Practice Entities

questions.title: When does a law practice's licence need to be reissued?
questions.text: When a law practice entity updates its particulars via LSRA e-Services, it can request for its licence to be reissued if there is a change in law practice's name or 'Valid From' date, with a fee of $50.
topics: Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals
Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals / Law Practice Entities

questions.title: What do we need to do if we want to change the business structure of our law practice?
questions.text:
Where a change in the business structure of your law practice requires a new UEN (e.g. from limited liability partnership to company), you will need to terminate your existing licence and apply for a new licence.
Both applications (for the termination and for the new law practice) should be concurrently submitted in advance. You can propose a future start date for the new law practice and a future termination date for the existing law practice. The licence of your existing law practice will continue to be valid until the termination date. To ensure continuity in your law practice's operations, please factor in the various processing time required when proposing the prospective start and end dates in the application forms.
Where there is no change in UEN, e.g. when a Singapore law practice ("SLP") changes from a sole proprietorship to partnership or vice versa (i.e. it remains a "law firm" as defined under the Legal Profession Act ("LPA")), it does not need to apply for a new licence. However, it should submit an application via LSRA e-Services to update the particulars of the business structure of the SLP.
Where a SLP partnership is becoming a sole proprietorship, it should take note of requirements under rule 8(1)(c) of the Legal Profession (Law Practice Entities) Rules 2015 in relation to the name of the law firm, and seek any necessary approvals via the update application. SLPs should also take note of the requirements under sections 157 and 159 of the LPA, where applicable.
Where there are registered lawyers in your law practice, their Certificates of Registration with your existing law practice will automatically lapse on the last day of validity of the licence. The new law practice will be required to apply for a new Certificate of Registration for the lawyers. The applications can be made as soon as the licence for the new law practice has been issued.
For questions relating to accountant's report under SLPs, please approach the Law Society of Singapore.
topics: Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals
Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals / Law Practice Entities

questions.title: How does a law corporation seek approval to amend provisions in its constitution?
questions.text:
Approval to amend provisions in the law corporation's constitution relating to or affecting the matters specified in the Second Schedule of the Legal Profession (Law Practice Entities) Rules 2015 should be sought by submitting an application to update via LSRA e-Services. Please upload a copy of the law practice's amended constitution (in Word format with tracked changes), with reasons for the proposed amendments, as a supporting document in the application.
Please note that your application may require more time to process if your constitution contains significant deviations from LSRA's specimen clauses and/or does not satisfy the legislative requirements.
topics: Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals
Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals / Law Practice Entities

questions.title: What do we need to do if we want to cease operation of our law practice?
questions.text:
If your law practice intends to cease operation , you will need to terminate your licence via LSRA e-Services before de-registering the entity with Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority.
You can submit the termination application in advance as you can propose a future termination date in the application form. The licence of your law practice will continue to be valid until the termination date.
If you plan to transition from one SLP to another, please also take note of the requirements under sections 157 and 159 of the Legal Profession Act, where applicable.
topics: Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals
Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals / Law Practice Entities

questions.title: Are there any requirements applicable to the use of law practice names in publicity or marketing materials, including websites and articles?
questions.text:
Law practices must use their full name corresponding with the approved name on their law practice licence, on all publicity materials including websites and articles written by the law practice's lawyers.
In particular, Singapore law practices ("SLP"), which are member firms of international networks or global firms or in any other collaborations with such firms, must ensure that they are referred to by their full names and their lawyers are properly listed as belonging to the SLP on the global or international website. The marketing and publicity materials should not give the impression that the SLP is a foreign law practice and must be consistent with the fact that the SLP is majority owned and controlled by Singapore lawyers, structured in compliance with the Legal Profession Act and subsidiary legislations.
topics: Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals
Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals / Law Practice Entities

questions.title: Our Singapore law practice ("SLP") intends to form a Joint Law Venture ("JLV") or a Formal Law Alliance ("FLA") with a foreign law practice ("FLP"). What are the requirements?
questions.text:
Please see the relevant rules and requirements relating to the formation of a JLV or FLA in Part IXA of the Legal Profession Act, read with the Legal Profession (Law Practice Entities) Rules 2015.
The FLA and JLV schemes were conceived as a means to facilitate cooperation between two independent law practice entities which are capable of dealing with each other as equal partners. The relevant legal framework for approval of these applications is interpreted and applied in this context.
In assessing whether a proposal complies with the requirement for a minimum number of Singapore solicitors in the SLP, the SLP is advised to ensure there are sufficient Singapore solicitors who have a track record that is independent of the FLP. For example, they should not have a history of employment with the FLP prior to the establishment of the FLA or JLV.
In addition, the law practices will require the minimum number of equity partners or directors as prescribed in the legislation. The SLP should also note the threshold requirements as set out in rule 3 of the Legal Profession (Law Practice Entities) Rules 2015.
topics: Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals
Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals / Law Practice Entities in Collaborations

questions.title: Can a Formal Law Alliance ("FLA") or Joint Law Venture ("JLV") comprise more than one law practice?
questions.text:
A FLA must comprise at least one Singapore law practice ("SLP") and one foreign law practice ("FLP") or Qualifying Foreign Law Practice ("QFLP").
A JLV can only comprise one SLP and one FLP or QFLP.
Please see the relevant provisions in the Legal Profession Act and Legal Profession (Law Practice Entities) Rules 2015.
topics: Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals
Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals / Law Practice Entities in Collaborations

questions.title: Are Formal Law Alliances and Joint Law Ventures allowed to have loans, service agreements?
questions.text: Please refer to the LSRA's Guidelines on Financial Arrangements Between Singapore Law Practices and Foreign Law Practices In Collaborations.

questions.title: How does a Formal Law Alliance ("FLA") or Joint Law Venture ("JLV") seek approval to amend its written agreement or business plan?
questions.text: Approval to amend a JLV's or FLA's written agreement or business plan should be sought by submitting an application to update via LSRA e-Services. Please upload a copy of the amended written agreement or business plan (in Word format with tracked changes), with reasons for the proposed amendments, as a supporting document in the application.

questions.title: If a member law practice joins or leaves a Group Practice, does the Group Practice need to apply for a new Certificate of Approval?
questions.text: No, however, the Group Practice will need to update their particulars via LSRA e-Services, and add or remove member law practices as applicable.

questions.title: Do we need to renew the approval under section 176(1) of the Legal Profession Act ("LPA")?
questions.text:
The approval will lapse if the foreign lawyer's registration is terminated (including a change to the lawyer's registration under the same law practice, e.g. from section 36C to section 36B of the LPA), cancelled or suspended or lapses. The Director of Legal Services can also cancel approval granted under section 176(1) of the LPA.
Please refer to our webpage on Apply to Approval to Hold Interests in a Law Practice Entity for more information.

Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals / Approval to Hold Interests in a Law Practice Entity

questions.title: Can a non-lawyer employee be a director, partner or shareholder in, or share in the profits of, a law practice?
questions.text:
The law practice will need to apply for approval. This may be done by submitting via LSRA e-Services:
(a) An application for approval to register the non-lawyer employee as a regulated non-practitioner ("RNP") under section 36G of the Legal Profession Act ("LPA"); and
(b) Concurrently, an application for approval to hold interests in a law practice if it is proposed for the individual to hold equity interests or voting rights in the law practice, or share in its profits.
Such non-lawyer participation in a law practice is subject to limits prescribed in the relevant legislation. The suitability of each individual is subject to fulfilment of certain requirements and will be assessed on a case-by-case basis. Please refer to section 36G of the LPA and the Legal Profession (Regulated Individuals) Rules 2015 (in particular Part 4) for more information. Singapore law practices should also note the threshold requirements in the Legal Profession (Law Practice Entities) Rules 2015.
Individuals with relevant expertise and experience, who can bring added value to a law practice in terms of transforming, advancing or contributing to its practice, or who are long-term employees of the law practice with a proven track record in the law practice, may be considered. The relevant areas of expertise of individuals who have been successfully registered to date include patents, competition and anti-trust, regulatory and compliance. The individual's proposed appointment in the law practice should be their sole employment.
Please note that RNPs are subject to the same disciplinary framework as lawyers in Singapore, including the Legal Profession (Professional Conduct) Rules 2015, under the LPA.
topics: Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals
Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals / Approval to Hold Interests in a Law Practice Entity

questions.title: Can we register our lawyers before we apply for a licence for a new law practice?
questions.text:
You will need to be issued a law practice licence by the Legal Services Regulatory Authority before you can apply for Certificates of Registration ("CoR") for your lawyers.
Estimated processing time is 30 working days. Applications with incomplete supporting documents/information, submitted during the peak period from December to April, and/or that are complex, will take longer to process. Complex applications include those involving concurrent appointments, foreign interests in Singapore law practices and/or collaborations between Singapore law practices and foreign law practice entities.
Please take the above timelines into account when proposing the commencement date(s) for your law practice licence and CoRs, and submit your applications in good time.
topics: Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals
Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals / Lawyers & Other Individuals

questions.title: How do I register as a foreign lawyer in Singapore? Which category should I choose?
questions.text:
Only licensed law practices in Singapore can apply to the Legal Services Regulatory Authority ("LSRA") to register foreign-qualified lawyers, who should be duly authorised or registered to practise law in a state or territory by an authority having the function conferred by law of authorising or registering persons to practise law in that state or territory.
A foreign-qualified lawyer who wishes to practise law in or from Singapore will need to first be offered employment by a licensed law practice in Singapore, which will then apply to the LSRA to register them as a foreign lawyer under the Legal Profession Act.
Please refer to the following links for more information:
Types of individual registration
Application process to register an individual
LSRA e-Services User Guide
topics: Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals
Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals / Lawyers & Other Individuals

questions.title: Can I be registered as a foreign lawyer if I can only engage in supervised legal practice? When will I be required and/or eligible to register as a foreign lawyer in Singapore?
questions.text:
Foreign-qualified lawyers who wish to provide legal services in or from a law practice in Singapore must be registered with the Legal Services Regulatory Authority ("LSRA").
LSRA only registers an individual who is duly authorised or registered to practise law in a state or territory other than Singapore by a foreign authority having the function conferred by law of authorising or registering persons to practise law in that state or territory. S/he must be qualified to practise independently in their principal jurisdiction and does not hold a restricted practising certificate.
Applications to register a foreign lawyer can only be submitted by a law practice licensed in Singapore.
topics: Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals
Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals / Lawyers & Other Individuals

questions.title: Does a foreign lawyer whose employer is an overseas law firm need to be registered with the Legal Services Regulatory Authority ("LSRA") if he works from the Singapore office?
questions.text: Under the Legal Profession Act, a foreign lawyer must not provide any legal services in or from Singapore through a licensed law practice entity unless s/he is registered with the LSRA.
topics: Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals
Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals / Lawyers & Other Individuals

questions.title: Can a Singapore law practice ("SLP") hire a foreign lawyer?
questions.text:
A SLP that wishes to employ a foreign lawyer can apply to the Legal Services Regulatory Authority ("LSRA") to register him or her under the Legal Profession Act.
Before doing so, the SLP should check that it meets the threshold requirements under rule 3 of the Legal Profession (Law Practice Entities) Rules 2015, and will continue to be able to meet those requirements should the registration be approved.
If it is intended for the foreign lawyer to be a partner, director or shareholder in, or to share in the profits of, the SLP, the SLP will also need to submit an application for approval for the foreign lawyer to hold interests in the SLP.
topics: Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals
Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals / Lawyers & Other Individuals

questions.title: Do I need to be registered with the Legal Services Regulatory Authority ("LSRA") if I am visiting Singapore on a temporary, ad-hoc basis for arbitration proceedings or hearings?
questions.text: Foreign lawyers who are visiting Singapore on a temporary, ad-hoc basis for arbitration proceedings or hearings, are not required to register with the LSRA as long as they are providing legal services in their own name or that of an overseas law practice, and not through a Singapore-based entity. Please note that such individuals will still need to comply with the Ministry of Manpower's work pass requirements.
topics: Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals
Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals / Lawyers & Other Individuals

questions.title: Do I need to be registered with the Legal Services Regulatory Authority ("LSRA") to work as an arbitrator or mediator in Singapore?
questions.text:
A person who acts only as an arbitrator in arbitration proceedings, or as a mediator in a mediation process, in Singapore will not be required to register with the LSRA.
Likewise, an entity comprising individuals who act only as arbitrators and/or mediators will not be required to register with the LSRA. If, however, the individual or entity intends to provide other services that extend beyond the scope of being an arbitrator or mediator, and which will involve the practice of law, such as providing legal advice and/or representing clients, they will be required to register with the LSRA as a lawyer or a law practice entity.
Please note that sections 32, 33 and 35 of the Legal Profession Act are separate from the applicable requirements to be registered or licences with the LSRA.
topics: Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals
Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals / Lawyers & Other Individuals

questions.title: Do in-house counsel need to be registered with the Legal Services Regulatory Authority ("LSRA")?
questions.text:
In-house counsel (also referred to as "legal counsel" or "corporate counsel") who are employed by an entity that is not a licensed law practice, are not required to register with the LSRA.
For other queries about in-house counsel, please contact the Singapore Corporate Counsel Association.
topics: Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals
Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals / Lawyers & Other Individuals

questions.title: Can a Singapore solicitor practise foreign law?
questions.text: Singapore solicitors practising in a Singapore law practice and those registered under section 36E of the Legal Profession Act ("LPA") in a foreign law practice entity, may, if they have dual qualifications, also practise the foreign law that they are qualified to practise in. While they need not hold an additional Certificate of Registration under section 36C of the LPA from the Legal Services Regulatory Authority, it is the individual's responsibility to ensure that their practice of foreign law accords with all relevant foreign jurisdictions.
topics: Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals
Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals / Lawyers & Other Individuals

questions.title: My law practice will not be able to provide an Accountant's Report in time for the renewal of my lawyer's registration period under section 36B/E of the Legal Profession Act. What do I need to submit?
questions.text: Please submit a letter of undertaking signed off by the Registrant, that your law practice will submit a copy of your accountant report that covers his/her current registration period in the next renewal application.
topics: Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals
Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals / Lawyers & Other Individuals

questions.title: When must we submit a Certificate of Good Standing ("CoGS") for lawyer registration applications?
questions.text:
CoGS is required for:
New applications for all Certificates of Registration ("CoR");
Renewal applications for CoRs under section 36B of the Legal Profession Act; and
If there is a change in the lawyer's principal jurisdiction.
It may also be requested for CoR renewal applications.
topics: Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals
Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals / Lawyers & Other Individuals

questions.title: Where can we find sample Continuing Professional Development ("CPD") declaration form and Certificate of Good Character ("CoGC"), to register a lawyer under section 36B of the Legal Profession Act?
questions.text: The CPD declaration form and sample CoGC can be found here.
topics: Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals
Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals / Lawyers & Other Individuals

questions.title: Do I still need a Singapore practising certificate ("PC") after obtaining a Certificate of Registration ("CoR") to practice in a foreign law practice entity?
questions.text:
Yes, all solicitors registered under section 36E of the Legal Profession Act must also have in force a PC in order to practise law.
If you have an existing PC, you are required to submit a Notice of Change of Particulars via Supreme Court's eLitigation system within 3 months from CoR start date to ensure that the law practice name and particulars are updated.
topics: Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals
Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals / Lawyers & Other Individuals

questions.title: How soon after being issued a Certificate of Registration must a foreign lawyer obtain a work pass?
questions.text:
If a foreign lawyer requires a work pass to work in Singapore, it must be obtained from the Ministry of Manpower within 6 months from the 'Valid from' date stated in the certificate of registration issued by the Legal Services Regulatory Authority.
For more information about work passes, please refer to the Ministry of Manpower's website.
topics: Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals
Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals / Lawyers & Other Individuals

questions.title: How early can we apply for a new (or to renew a) Certificate of Registration ("CoR")?
questions.text: To ensure that particulars and documents submitted remain up to date, please submit CoR applications not more than 6 months before the lawyer's proposed commencement date at your law practice.
topics: Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals
Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals / Lawyers & Other Individuals

questions.title: What happens if my lawyer's certificate of registration ("CoR") has expired?
questions.text:
If your law practice did not submit an application to renew the CoR before its expiry, it will need to submit an application for a new CoR. Please do so as soon as possible. Please note that providing legal services in or from Singapore without a valid CoR is prohibited under the Legal Profession Act. The lawyer should not practise law in or from Singapore unless and until a new CoR has been issued.
If the lawyer's renewal application is submitted via LSRA e-Services before the existing CoR has expired, the renewed CoR will be valid from the day after the existing CoR expires, even if the existing CoR expires before the renewed CoR is issued.
It is the responsibility of the Registrant and the law practice to take note of the expiry date and ensure that CoR applications are submitted in good time. Applications can be submitted up to 6 months in advance.
topics: Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals
Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals / Lawyers & Other Individuals

questions.title: Can a lawyer's certificate of registration ("CoR") be backdated?
questions.text: No, for applications to the Legal Services Regulatory Authority ("LSRA") submitted for a new CoR for a lawyer, the CoR will be valid from the date it is issued by the LSRA, or a later date requested by the law practice in the application.
topics: Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals
Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals / Lawyers & Other Individuals

questions.title: I am a registered lawyer who will be moving to a different law practice. How do I transfer my Certificate of Registration ("CoR")?
questions.text:
The CoR of a lawyer moving from his/her current law practice to another law practice cannot be transferred.
The other law practice will need to apply for a new CoR for the lawyer, and the lawyer's current law practice will need to submit an application to terminate his/her existing CoR.
For continuity of practice, both applications can be submitted concurrently and in advance as the law practices can enter prospective start or end dates in the application forms. Please also factor in the various processing time required when proposing the prospective start and end dates in the application forms. Your CoR registered under your current law practice will continue to be valid until the termination date.
Please note that we will only be able to issue the new CoR after we have received and processed the application to terminate the existing CoR from the lawyer's current law practice.
A Singapore solicitor, who is registered under section 36E of the Legal Profession Act, moving from a foreign law practice entity to a Singapore law practice will not need a CoR at the Singapore law practice. However, the foreign law practice entity will need to terminate his/her CoR.
topics: Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals
Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals / Lawyers & Other Individuals

questions.title: How do we change a lawyer's registration type (e.g. from section 36C of the Legal Profession Act to section 36B) under the same law practice?
questions.text:
Your law practice will need to register the lawyer under the new registration type, and concurrently submit an application to terminate his/her existing Certificate of Registration ("CoR").
For continuity of practice, both applications can be submitted concurrently and in advance as your law practice can enter prospective start or end dates in the application forms. Please also factor in the various processing time required when proposing the prospective start and end dates in the application forms. The existing CoR of the lawyer will continue to be valid until the termination date.
Please note that we will only be able to issue the new CoR after we have received and processed the application to terminate the existing CoR.
topics: Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals
Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals / Lawyers & Other Individuals

questions.title: How do we update the particulars of a foreign lawyer or regulated non-practitioner?
questions.text:
Update applications should be submitted before, or within 7 days after, any change in the individual's particulars.
Please refer to our webpage: Update the Particulars of an Individual for more information.

Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals / Lawyers & Other Individuals

questions.title: Does a Singapore law practice need to update Legal Services Regulatory Authority ("LSRA") regarding the particulars of Singapore solicitors?
questions.text:
Yes, if the Singapore solicitor is a Managing Partner/Director of the Singapore law practice. All other matters relating to Singapore solicitors are under the purview of the Supreme Court.
Singapore solicitors practising in Singapore law practices should continue to submit a Notice of Change of Particulars via eLitigation to update their particulars.
LSRA has a data interface with the Supreme Court, so the information submitted to the Supreme Court will be transmitted to LSRA, and our records and search function will be automatically updated after 1 or 2 working days.
topics: Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals
Licensing or Registration of Law Practice Entities/Individuals / Lawyers & Other Individuals

questions.title: In what circumstances does a lawyer's certificate of registration ("CoR") need to be reissued?
questions.text: When a law practice updates the particulars of a lawyer or regulated non-practitioner via LSRA e-Services, it can request that the individual's CoR be reissued if any of the fields in the certificate is being updated, e.g. the individual's name, law practice's name, with a fee of $50.

questions.title: Can a foreign lawyer obtain a copy of their previous Certificate(s) of Registration ("CoRs")?
questions.text:
Generally, the Legal Services Regulatory Authority ("LSRA") does not issue copies of previous CoR (including those issued by the Attorney-General's Chambers' Legal Profession Secretariat prior to the establishment of the LSRA in November 2015).
If you require proof that you were registered as a foreign lawyer in Singapore for a particular period, you can request a Certificate of Good Standing instead.

questions.title: How do we terminate the registration of a lawyer or a section 36G regulated non-practitioner?
questions.text:
Please submit a termination application via LSRA e-Services.
Termination applications should be submitted before, or within 7 days after, the individual's last day of employment with the law practice.
The practising certificates of Singapore solicitors registered under section 36E of the LPA should be cancelled via the Supreme Court's eLitigation system.

questions.title: Does my law practice have to terminate the Certificate of Registration ("CoR") of a lawyer who will be seconded?
questions.text: The lawyer should retain the CoR if s/he continues to provide legal services through the law practice entity that s/he is registered with, and be covered by the law practice's professional indemnity insurance.

questions.title: What is the Legal Aid Bureau (LAB)?
questions.text:
The Legal Aid Bureau (LAB) is a department of Singapore's Ministry of Law, headed by the Director of Legal Aid. It was set up in 1958 to provide quality legal aid, advice and assistance in civil law matters to the less privileged.
For more information about LAB, please refer to our website.
topics: Legal Aid (General Information) / Scope of Work and Services

questions.title: Where is LAB located?
questions.text:
We are located at 45 Maxwell Road, The URA Centre (East Wing), #07-11, Singapore 069118.
Before visiting the Bureau, please make an appointment via the OneMinLaw Portal (OMP) at https://go.gov.sg/omp to reduce waiting time.
topics: Legal Aid (General Information) / Scope of Work and Services

questions.title: What are the services provided by LAB?
questions.text:
LAB provides the following services:
Legal Advice - Oral advice on questions relating to Singapore law and the practical steps you may take for your case.
Legal Assistance - Drafting of Wills and Deeds of Separation.
Legal Aid - Representation in various civil proceedings as set out in the Legal Aid and Advice Act, including proceedings before the Court of Appeal, the High Court, District Courts, Magistrates' Courts, the Family Courts, the Syariah Court and the Syariah Court Appeal Board, and the Commissioner of Labour under the Work Injury Compensation Act.
topics: Legal Aid (General Information) / Scope of Work and Services

questions.title: What types of cases are not handled by LAB?
questions.text:
Criminal Proceedings
LAB does not handle criminal proceedings.
If you require legal advice or representation in criminal proceedings, you may wish to approach the Public Defender's Office or Pro Bono SG.
Certain Civil Proceedings
LAB does not handle certain civil proceedings including the following:
Defamation cases
Proceedings before the Small Claims Tribunal and the Tribunal for the Maintenance of Parents
Mediation at the Tripartite Alliance for Dispute Management and proceedings before the Employment Claims Tribunal
Generally, LAB also does not handle proceedings in the Family Court for Maintenance and Personal Protection Orders where the opposing party is not legally represented, unless there are exceptional circumstances (e.g. the Applicant is a vulnerable person who has a physical or mental disability)
topics: Legal Aid (General Information) / Scope of Work and Services

questions.title: What languages can LAB officers speak?
questions.text: LAB officers are able to conduct interviews and provide legal advice in the national languages, namely English, Malay, Tamil, Mandarin, and in Chinese dialects such as Teochew, Hokkien, and Cantonese.
topics: Legal Aid (General Information) / Scope of Work and Services

questions.title: Can LAB assist me in on-going court proceedings, if I previously had a private solicitor but cannot afford to continue paying legal fees?
questions.text:
Yes. In such cases, we will require you to provide us with a letter of discharge from your private solicitor.
Further, should there be any court dates such as Case Conferences while we are still processing your application for legal aid, you will have to attend court yourself to seek an adjournment.
topics: Legal Aid (General Information) / Scope of Work and Services

questions.title: Do I qualify for legal aid?
questions.text:
Legal aid is available to Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents who are resident and present in Singapore, as well as citizens or residents of contracting states who are involved in applications under The Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction (HCCAICA).
If you are below the age of 21, your parent or guardian must apply on your behalf.
Legal aid applicants must also satisfy a Means Test and a Merits Test before they can receive legal aid.
If you are a citizen or resident of one of the contracting states of the HCCAICA and wish to apply for legal aid, please approach the Singapore Central Authority to assist you in your application, as all such applications must be made through the Singapore Central Authority.
topics: Legal Aid (General Information) / Eligibility for Aid - Means Testing

questions.title: If I am a bankrupt, can I still apply for legal aid or legal advice?
questions.text: You are eligible to apply for legal aid or legal advice even though you are a bankrupt, subject to satisfying our Means and Merits Tests. However, we will need to obtain the Official Assignee's approval in order to commence certain types of court proceedings for you, namely those which would affect the assets in your bankruptcy estate (excluding divorce proceedings and personal injury claims).
topics: Legal Aid (General Information) / Eligibility for Aid - Means Testing

questions.title: What is the Means Test for legal aid applicants?
questions.text:
The Means Test assesses your financial circumstances to determine if you are of limited means. This will be conducted shortly after you submit your application for legal aid.
Applicants for legal aid must meet the following criteria:
a. The average Per Capita Gross Monthly Household Income (PCHI) must be $1,050 or lower for the last 12 months prior to the application;
b. The Annual Value of the applicant's place of residence owned by the applicant must be $21,000 or lower; and
c. The applicant's savings and non-CPF investments must be $10,000 or lower, if he is younger than 60 years old. Applicants aged 60 and above are allowed to have savings and non-CPF investments of $40,000 or lower.
The applicant must not own any other property besides his/her place of residence.
You will be required to swear a Statutory Declaration before a Commissioner for Oaths as to your means.
A person who knowingly makes any false statement or representation to LAB shall be guilty of an offence and shall be liable on conviction to a fine of up to $5,000 or imprisonment of up to six months or to both.
topics: Legal Aid (General Information) / Eligibility for Aid - Means Testing

questions.title: What is the average Per Capita Monthly Household Income under the Means Test for legal aid applicants?
questions.text:
The average Per Capita Monthly Household Income (PCHI) is the average gross household income for the last 12 months divided by the total number of household members (including the applicant).
"Gross income" refers to the gross wages or salaries before deduction of CPF contributions and personal income tax. It comprises basic wages, overtime pay, commissions, tips, other allowances and bonuses. For self-employed persons, gross income refers to profits from their business, trade or profession (i.e. total receipts less business expenses incurred) before the deduction of income tax.
"Household members" refers to persons related by blood, marriage and/or legal adoption and have the same residential address reflected on the NRIC as the applicant for legal aid. Your spouse's income may be disregarded in certain situations e.g. applications for divorce proceedings.
The MinLaw Services Centre will calculate the average PCHI as part of the means test, based on the supporting documents provided by the applicant for legal aid.
topics: Legal Aid (General Information) / Eligibility for Aid - Means Testing

questions.title: Do I take the Means Test online or in person?
questions.text:
Legal Advice Case
If you register for a legal advice case online, you are required to do the Means Test online. If you attend at LAB to register for a legal advice case, you are required to do the Means Test at the Bureau's registration counter.
Legal Aid/Assistance Case
If you register for a legal aid or legal assistance case online, you are required to attend at LAB within the next 2 working days to do a preliminary Means Test at the registration counter. After you have passed the preliminary Means Test, you will be given a Means Test appointment for your means to be formally assessed.
If you attend at LAB to register for a legal aid or legal assistance case, you are required to do a preliminary Means Test at the registration counter. After you have passed the preliminary Means Test, you will be given a Means Test appointment for your means to be formally assessed.
If you are attending at the Bureau to register a legal advice/assistance case or legal aid, please make an appointment via the OneMinLaw Portal (OMP) at https://go.gov.sg/omp to reduce waiting time.
topics: Legal Aid (General Information) / Eligibility for Aid - Means Testing

questions.title: What can I do if I have already approached LAB and am found to be above means?
questions.text: In such a situation, LAB will not be able to further assist you. You may wish to approach a private solicitor for legal representation or act for yourself.
topics: Legal Aid (General Information) / Above Means - Other Sources of Help

questions.title: If I fail the Means Test, can I still obtain legal aid if I face financial hardship?
questions.text: If you fail the means test but you have certain reasons or information that you think makes your situation different or special, for example if you have a very serious illness and cannot afford legal services as you need to pay for major medical procedures, you may contact the MinLaw Services Centre for further assistance.
topics: Legal Aid (General Information) / Above Means - Other Sources of Help

questions.title: Where else can I get help if I do not qualify for civil legal aid with LAB?
questions.text:
If you want legal advice, you may wish to refer to the following list of legal clinics in Singapore.
You may also refer to this link for the assistance available at the Pro Bono SG.
If you want a practising lawyer, please refer to the online resources section in the following link.
topics: Legal Aid (General Information) / Above Means - Other Sources of Help

questions.title: What is the Merits Test for legal aid applicants?
questions.text:
The Merits Test assesses whether you have a reasonable case to bring or defend in court.
After Statement Taking is done, and all the necessary documents for your case have been received by LAB, a lawyer will be assigned to investigate your case. He may ask for further information and documents from you to understand your case better. He will then put up an opinion on the merits of your case. This opinion will be put before the Legal Aid Board for their consideration on whether to grant you legal aid.
If the Legal Aid Board is of the view that your case has merits, i.e. you have a reasonable case to bring or defend in court, then it will grant you legal aid.
However, if the Board is of the view that your case does not have merits, then it will not grant you legal aid.
LAB will send you a letter letting you know whether you have been granted legal aid. If you have not been granted legal aid, then the letter will briefly explain the reasons for this.
With effect from 16 October 2019, the Director for Legal Aid can, without reference to the Legal Aid Board, approve applications for legal aid in certain types of cases e.g. uncontested adoption proceedings, simple uncontested divorce proceedings, non-disputed proceedings for grant of letters of administration or probate. *Do note that you will still have to pass the Means Test and show that you have a meritorious case for aid to be granted.
All decisions of the Legal Aid Board and/or the Director of Legal Aid in respect of applications for legal aid are final.

questions.title: What is the Legal Aid Board?
questions.text: The Legal Aid Board comprises the Director of Legal Aid and at least two other independent solicitors who are on LAB's Panel of Assigned Solicitors.

questions.title: When can legal aid be refused or cancelled?
questions.text:
The Director of Legal Aid may refuse legal aid, even if the applicant has passed the means and merits tests, if it appears to him unreasonable that the applicant should receive it in the particular circumstances of the case, for example if there is a third party whose interests are aligned with the applicant's, who could afford to fund the litigation, and who would also benefit from the litigation.
In addition to the Director of Legal Aid's discretion to refuse legal aid, the Legal Aid Board may cancel the legal aid previously granted to you, for various reasons, for example:
Where you have failed to pay your assessed contribution or any payment due to LAB for more than 30 days after the time you were supposed to pay
Where LAB finds out new information, or your circumstances change, and this new information/the changed circumstances means that you are no longer financially eligible for legal aid
Where your lawyer assesses that you no longer have any reasonable grounds to bring, continue with or defend a case in court
Generally, where it is unreasonable for you to continue receiving legal aid. For example, you refuse to accept your lawyer's advice or comply with Court directions, you remain uncontactable despite numerous attempts by LAB to contact you, you have been abusive towards your lawyer, you have refused to provide information your lawyer has asked you for, or provided false information etc.

questions.title: What happens after legal aid is cancelled?
questions.text:
We will inform you that you will no longer be legally represented by LAB and proceed to close your file.
If you have ongoing Court proceedings, you will have to decide whether you wish to continue with your case in person or to engage a private lawyer to represent you. If no action is taken on your part to continue with your case, the Court may eventually strike out your case or your defence, or make any decision in the matter as it sees fit.

questions.title: Is legal aid free?
questions.text:
You do not have to pay if you wish to seek legal advice from our Duty Lawyer.
However, legal aid is not free. Most applicants will be required to pay a contribution towards the costs of work done for legal assistance or legal aid matters.
The contribution payable is assessed having regard to an applicant's financial means, the nature of the case, the amount of work done and the amount of money recovered. The assessed contribution amount is unlikely to exceed $1,650. You will usually be required to pay a first instalment before any work is started on your case and a second instalment after your case has been completed.
topics: Legal Aid (General Information) / Payment of Contribution for Legal Aid

questions.title: How much contribution towards legal aid will I be required to pay?
questions.text:
The total contribution usually does not exceed $1,650, but it may be more in some cases. You will usually be asked to pay a first instalment before any work is started on your case and a second instalment after your case has been completed.
We will usually start representing you in Court only after you have paid your first contribution.
If your case is assigned to an Assigned Solicitor, you will not need to pay the Assigned Solicitor's bill. However, if you receive a judgment or settlement sum in your case, LAB will be required to withhold certain amounts from this sum from you, which includes an amount representing the Assigned Solicitor's bill.
topics: Legal Aid (General Information) / Payment of Contribution for Legal Aid

questions.title: How do I pay my assessed contribution and/or other charges to LAB?
questions.text:
You can make payment through the following methods:
a. Come down to LAB to pay by NETS
b. Pay online through the Applicant Portal:
i. Click on "For Applicants",
ii. Click on "here" in the sentence "Click here to register a new case or login to your existing case",
iii. Login with your Singpass, and
iv. Click on "Payment" at the bar on the left.
c. Pay through a bank transfer: Please use these bank transfer details:
Bank Account Name: Legal Aid Bureau/AG
Bank Name: DBS Bank Ltd Account Number: 001-073506-3
Bank Code: 7171
Branch Code: 001
Remarks: Please indicate our case reference number under the "Remarks" section when making the transfer. Once the transfer is done, please send us a screenshot of the completed payment via the Applicant Portal or the enquiry form under "Contact Us" at https://www.mlaw.gov.sg.
topics: Legal Aid (General Information) / Payment of Contribution for Legal Aid

questions.title: Do I have to pay for anything other than the assessed contribution?
questions.text: You have to pay for the expenses of obtaining documents that are essential to your case, such as medical reports, expert opinions or searches, as well as for fees incurred in the service of Court documents on the opposing party.
topics: Legal Aid (General Information) / Payment of Contribution for Legal Aid

questions.title: What should I do if I am unable to pay the required contribution towards legal aid?
questions.text:
If you are unable to pay the assessed contribution towards legal aid in full, you may request to pay in instalments.
If you would like the contribution to be reduced or waived, you may submit your appeal together with relevant supporting documents to show your financial difficulties.
Please submit your completed Instalment Payment Plan Form or Reduction/Waiver Form via Contact Us @ OneMinLaw.
topics: Legal Aid (General Information) / Payment of Contribution for Legal Aid

questions.title: Can a person who has been granted legal aid visit casinos?
questions.text:
From 1 August 2013, if you are granted legal aid, you will be subject to Third-Party Casino Exclusion. Under Third-Party Casino Exclusion, you may not enter or remain or take part in any gaming on any local casino premises.
The Third-Party Casino Exclusion will remain in force until all your active legal aid cases are closed. Please note that until the casino operator is notified of the termination of your Third-Party Casino Exclusion, you can be refused entry into the local casinos. For more information on Casino Exclusion, please call the National Problem Gambling Helpline at 1800 6668 668*.
*Airtime charges may apply to calls made from mobile phones to ‘1800’ local toll-free numbers.
topics: Legal Aid (General Information) / Conditions and Benefits of Receiving Legal Aid

questions.title: What other benefits are there for legally aided persons?
questions.text:
Other than receiving subsidised legal representation, legally aided persons also have certain benefits. A legally aided person:
Is not liable for Court fees, fees of process server and any fees due to the Sheriff or bailiff;
Is entitled to be supplied free of charge with a copy of the judge's notes of evidence; and
Is not liable for costs to any other party even if he or she does not succeed in their claim or defence, except in certain limited circumstances provided under the Legal Aid & Advice Act, for example, if the Court decides that the legally aided person has obtained legal aid through fraud or misrepresentation or has acted improperly in the conduct of their Court proceedings.
topics: Legal Aid (General Information) / Conditions and Benefits of Receiving Legal Aid

questions.title: How do I apply for legal advice?
questions.text:
If you require legal advice, you can come to LAB during our office hours (8.30am to 5.00pm) to make an application. We are closed on weekends and Public Holidays. Please bring along your Identity Card for the registration.
Alternatively, you can make an online application here for selected subject matters. Once you have made your application for legal advice online with LAB, please visit LAB within 3 working days from date of registration to see our officer. We can assist you after you pass the Means test.
If you are a minor (i.e. a person below 21 years of age), your parent or guardian must apply on your behalf.
Before visiting the Bureau, please make an appointment via the OneMinLaw Portal (OMP) at https://go.gov.sg/omp to reduce waiting time.
topics: Legal Aid and Advice Process / Legal Advice

questions.title: Do I have to attend at LAB to get legal advice? Are there other locations to seek legal advice without travelling to LAB?
questions.text:
LAB has collaborated with Social Service Offices, Family Service Centres and Community Clubs to provide legal advice via videoconferencing at various locations.
You may check with your social worker for the locations of these community touchpoints that have a videoconferencing arrangement with LAB.
Alternatively, you can refer to this link to view the list of the community touchpoints with videoconferencing arrangements with LAB.
topics: Legal Aid and Advice Process / Legal Advice

questions.title: How do I apply for legal aid or legal assistance?
questions.text:
If you require legal aid or legal assistance, you can come to LAB during our office hours (8.30am to 5.00pm) to make an application. We are closed on weekends and Public Holidays. Please bring along your Identity Card for the registration.
Alternatively, you can make an online application here for selected subject matters. Once you have made your application for legal aid or legal assistance online with LAB, please visit LAB within 3 working days from date of registration to see our officer who will advise on whether a file can be opened. We can assist you after you pass the Means and Merits test. (The Merits test applies only for legal aid applications, not legal assistance applications.)
If you are a minor (i.e. a person below 21 years of age), your parent or guardian must apply on your behalf.
Before visiting the Bureau, please make an appointment via the OneMinLaw Portal (OMP) at https://go.gov.sg/omp to reduce waiting time.
topics: Legal Aid and Advice Process / Legal Aid/Legal Assistance

questions.title: What is the legal aid or legal assistance application process like and what are the timelines?
questions.text:
Please note that this is a general overview of LAB's application process for legal aid and assistance. Your application may be processed differently, depending on the facts of your case.* In addition, the Merits test does not apply to legal assistance matters.
The timeline for your case depends on the complexity of your case and the amount of time needed to assess your case. For legal aid matters, your legal officer has to review your statement, research the legal position and draft an opinion for submission to the Board. In general, it will take about three to four months.
*Note: This is not applicable to applications under The Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction (HCCAICA). If you are a citizen or resident of one of the contracting states of the HCCAICA and wish to apply for legal aid, please approach the Singapore Central Authority to assist you in your application. After you have applied through the Singapore Central Authority, your case will be referred to LAB and will go through the means test, statement taking and merits test stages before aid is granted or refused.
topics: Legal Aid and Advice Process / Legal Aid/Legal Assistance

questions.title: What documents should I bring in order to register for legal aid?
questions.text:
Please bring your NRIC or passport. You should also bring all documents relevant to your case. For example, if you are being sued, please bring all of the court documents that you have received. This will allow the legal officer to give you the appropriate advice.
If you are applying for divorce, for example, please bring with you the following:
Original Marriage Certificate
Original Children's Birth Certificate
Court documents eg. Expedited Orders, Personal Protection Orders, Maintenance Orders, if any
Information on NRIC number, last known contact number and address of spouse
Latest HDB / bank mortgage statement of account, if applicable
Latest CPF Public Housing Statement, if applicable
Please ensure that you have your SingPass password with you as you may need to access your SingPass account.
Before visiting the Bureau, please make an appointment via the OneMinLaw Portal (OMP) at https://go.gov.sg/omp to reduce waiting time.
topics: Legal Aid and Advice Process / Legal Aid/Legal Assistance

questions.title: How do I submit documents to LAB online for my case?

questions.title: What will my legal aid lawyer do for my case?
questions.text:
If you qualify for legal aid, our LAB lawyer or Assigned Solicitor will prepare your court documents and arrange for you to sign them.
He or she will liaise with the opposing party or their lawyer, represent you in Court, and inform you when you have to be present for Court proceedings. He or she will also keep you updated of all significant steps that are being taken to complete your case. LAB will also monitor the progress of your case if it is being handled by an Assigned Solicitor.
topics: Legal Aid and Advice Process / Your Legal Aid Lawyer

questions.title: Who will my legal aid lawyer be?
questions.text:
Your legal aid lawyer will either be a lawyer from LAB, or an Assigned Solicitor on LAB's panel of Assigned Solicitors.
Generally, LAB assigns cases to Assigned Solicitors in situations such as the following:
There is a conflict of interest, because both parties have applied for legal aid;
The case involves a specialised area of law, such as Syariah law or medical negligence; or
The case is particularly time-sensitive, e.g. an appeal matter.
topics: Legal Aid and Advice Process / Your Legal Aid Lawyer

questions.title: Can I choose my own Assigned Solicitor?
questions.text:
LAB is running a 'Choose your own Assigned Solicitor' Programme which allows applicants of legal aid to choose their preferred Assigned Solicitor. However, this programme is only open to applicants who wish to initiate civil divorce proceedings and have not commenced proceedings yet.
More details about the programme and the list of our participating Assigned Solicitors can be found here.
For other queries about this programme, please refer to this link.
For all other cases, LAB will choose an Assigned Solicitor for you, based on various factors, such as the Assigned Solicitor's area of expertise and language spoken.
topics: Legal Aid and Advice Process / Your Legal Aid Lawyer

questions.title: I am unable to log in to LAB's e-services/Portals. Who should I contact?
questions.text:
You will need a valid SingPass account to access the e-services portal on our website.
If you have problems accessing your SingPass account, please visit www.singpass.gov.sg for more information. You can also contact the SingPass Helpdesk at 6643 0555 for assistance.
If the access problems are unrelated to your SingPass account, please contact the MinLaw Service Centre at Tel: 1800 CALL LAW (1800 225 5529*) or +65 6225 5529 (for overseas callers) for assistance.

questions.title: What should I do if I missed my scheduled appointments with LAB? Can I cancel/reschedule my appointment?
questions.text:

questions.title: Who should I contact if I have questions about my legal aid case?
questions.text:
You may contact LAB at 1800-2255-529* or online at Contact Us @ OneMinlaw if you have any queries relating to your case, including its progress.
If your case is assigned to an Assigned Solicitor, we will inform you of the name of your Assigned Solicitor, his office address and contact number. You may contact your Assigned Solicitor directly regarding any queries relating to your case.
* Airtime charges may apply to calls made from mobile phones to ‘1800’ local toll-free numbers.
topics: Legal Aid and Advice Process / Working on Your Legal Aid Case

questions.title: When is my case considered to be completed?
questions.text: Your case will be completed after the Court proceedings have concluded. This may be after the Court has made an order, or when the parties have settled the matter out of Court, or if either party has withdrawn or discontinued the Court proceedings.
topics: Legal Aid and Advice Process / Working on Your Legal Aid Case

questions.title: How long will it take to complete my legal aid case?
questions.text:
The time needed to complete your case depends on a number of factors, e.g. the legal and factual complexity of the case, and whether the opposing party is legally represented and contesting the case.
Each case is unique and the time taken to complete your case will vary. However, as a rough estimate, straightforward cases (e.g. an uncontested divorce case where parties are able to agree on ancillary issues) will usually take less than 12 months to complete.
topics: Legal Aid and Advice Process / Working on Your Legal Aid Case

questions.title: How can I speed up the completion of my case?
questions.text:
You must be responsible for the progress of your case and cooperate with your LAB lawyer or assigned solicitor (i.e. a volunteer lawyer on LAB's panel of solicitors) in order to expedite the progress of your case.
For example, when you are required to submit documents or attend appointments with your LAB lawyer or assigned solicitor, you must do so punctually. When you are informed to attend Court proceedings, you must do so.
It is also important for you to update us on your latest correspondence address and your contact numbers so that we will be able to contact you.
topics: Legal Aid and Advice Process / Working on Your Legal Aid Case

questions.title: How do I withdraw my application for legal aid?
questions.text:
You can inform the officer in charge of your case that you wish to withdraw your case.
Please note that you may still have to pay contribution assessed for your case.
topics: Legal Aid and Advice Process / Working on Your Legal Aid Case

questions.title: Will I be paid or have to pay costs if I win or lose my legally aided case?
questions.text:
If you win the case, the Court may order costs to be paid by the opposing party to the Director of Legal Aid.
Legally aided persons will usually not be ordered by the Court to pay costs if you lose the case. However, there may be situations in which the Court may order you to pay costs. For example, if the Court decides that you have obtained legal aid through fraud or misrepresentation or that you have acted improperly in the conduct of your Court proceedings, it may order you to pay costs to the opposing party.
topics: Legal Aid and Advice Process / Working on Your Legal Aid Case

questions.title: How do I appeal against the Court's decision or order with regards to my legally aided case?
questions.text:
If you wish to appeal, you must go down to LAB immediately after the Court has given its decision or order. This is because there are strict timelines for the filing of an appeal and LAB will not be able to assist you to file the Notice of Appeal (NOA) if there is very little time left to do so. If you were represented for your case, you should also find out from your lawyer when the deadline to file the NOA is.
Please note that LAB can only assist if there is at least 5 working days before the deadline to file the NOA.
topics: Legal Aid and Advice Process / Working on Your Legal Aid Case

If you are unsure, you should obtain legal advice from your solicitor as to whether your intended business activity amounts to moneylending for which a licence is required.

questions.title: What should I consider before taking up a loan?
questions.text:
You should keep these key points in mind:
Before approaching a moneylender, consider other alternatives, such as the various financial assistance schemes offered by various Government agencies. You may contact the agencies to find out more about their schemes.
You are legally obliged to fulfil any loan contract you enter into with a licensed moneylender.
Consider whether you are able to abide by the contractual terms, bearing in mind your income and financial obligations. Borrow only what you need and are able to repay. Be mindful that if you are unable to meet the contractual terms, the late payment fees and interest payment will be a financial strain not just on yourself but also on your family.
The law requires moneylenders to explain the terms of a loan to you in a language you understand and to provide you with a copy of the loan contract. Make sure you fully understand the terms of the contract, in particular, the repayment schedule, the interest rate charged and the fees applicable.
Consider carefully before agreeing to any contractual term which allows a moneylender to lodge a caveat on the sale proceeds of your real estate property upon default of the loan repayment. When a caveat is lodged against your property, you will not be able to sell it without first repaying the moneylender in full. If the repayment is taken from the net proceeds from the sale of the property, it can wipe out all or a substantial portion of the proceeds.
You should shop around different moneylenders for the most favourable terms. You should not rush into and commit yourself to a loan until you are satisfied with the terms and conditions.

questions.title: What are the interest rates moneylenders can charge?
questions.text:
With effect from 1 October 2015, the maximum interest rate moneylenders can charge is 4% per month. This cap applies regardless of the borrower's income and whether the loan is an unsecured or secured one. If a borrower fails to repay the loan on time, the maximum rate of late interest a moneylender can charge is 4% per month for each month the loan is repaid late.
The computation of interest charged on the loan must be based on the amount of principal remaining after deducting from the original principal the total payments made by or on behalf of the borrower which are appropriated to principal. [To illustrate, if X takes a loan of $10,000, and X has repaid $4,000, only the remaining $6,000 can be taken into account for the computation of interest.]
The late interest can only be charged on an amount that is repaid late. The moneylender cannot charge on amounts that are outstanding but not yet due to be repaid. [To illustrate, if X takes a loan of $10,000, and fails to pay for the first instalment of $2,000, the moneylender may charge the late interest on $2,000 but not on the remaining $8,000 as it is not due yet.]

questions.title: What are the fees that moneylenders can charge?
questions.text:
With effect from 1 October 2015, all moneylenders are only permitted to impose the following charges and expenses:
a fee not exceeding $60 for each month of late repayment;
a fee not exceeding 10% of the principal of the loan when a loan is granted; and
legal costs ordered by the court for a successful claim by the moneylender for the recovery of the loan.
The total charges imposed by a moneylender on any loan, consisting of interest, late interest, upfront administrative and late fee also cannot exceed an amount equivalent to the principal of the loan. [To illustrate, if X takes a loan of $10,000, then the interest, late interest, 10% administrative fee and monthly $60 late fees cannot exceed $10,000.]

questions.title: How do I know whether a moneylender is licensed or not?
questions.text:
Do not borrow from unlicensed moneylenders. Verify that a moneylender is licensed in Singapore by checking the list of licensed moneylenders. Click here to access the list of licensed moneylenders. The list also shows the approved place(s) of business for each licensed moneylender.
Notwithstanding that the moneylenders are licensed, be mindful if they:
Use abusive language, or behave in a threatening manner towards you.
Ask for your SingPass user ID and/or password.
Retain your NRIC card or any other personal ID documents (e.g. driver’s licence, passport, work permit, employment pass or ATM card).
Ask you to sign on a blank or incomplete Note of Contract for the loan.
Grant you a loan without giving you a copy of the Note of contract for the loan and/or without properly explaining to you all the terms and conditions.
Grant you a loan without exercising due diligence (e.g. approving a loan over the phone, SMS or email before even receiving your loan application form and supporting documents, such as the income tax assessment and payslips).
Withhold any part of your principal loan amount for any reason.
Such practices are not acceptable. If you encounter them, you should report the moneylender to the Registry of Moneylenders, with information such as the moneylender’s business name, licence and contact numbers. Please see "How do I make a complaint about a moneylender?" for more details.
To find out more about unlicensed moneylenders, you may click on this link: Unlicensed Moneylending

questions.title: How can I tell whether an advertisement is from a licensed moneylender or an unlicensed moneylender?
questions.text:
Under the Registrar’s Directions On Advertising & Marketing Activities Of Licensed Moneylenders, which took effect on 1 November 2011, licensed moneylenders are permitted to advertise only through these three channels: (a) business or consumer directories (in print or online media); (b) websites belonging to the moneylender; and (c) advertisements placed within or on the exterior of the moneylender’s business premises. All other channels are prohibited.
In this regard, the advertising rules can help you differentiate between licensed and unlicensed moneylenders. If you receive flyers, SMSes, emails or other forms of advertisements which are not permitted under the rules, these would be from either licensed moneylenders operating in violation of the rules, or unlicensed moneylenders. Hence, you are advised not to respond to such advertisements. Instead, you should report the advertisements to the Registry at 1800-2255-529* or via Contact Us @ OneMinLaw. Errant licensed moneylenders will be investigated by the Registry and unlicensed moneylenders will be investigated by the Police.
*When calling the MinLaw Enquiry Line using the 1800 2255 529, please note that airtime charges may apply to calls made from mobile phones

questions.title: Can I rely on the content of an advertisement to take up a loan from a moneylender?
questions.text: You are advised to seek clarifications on specific terms of the loan contract before signing up with a licensed moneylender, and not to rely solely on the content of advertisements from the moneylender.

questions.title: In the event that I am standing as a surety for a loan, what should I look out for?
What should I do after being granted a loan?
questions.text:
Make sure the moneylender delivers to you the correct principal amount of the loan. The moneylender is only permitted an upfront deduction of a loan approval fee of up to 10% of the principal amount.
Pay the loan instalments on time to avoid incurring late payment fees and late interest.
Make sure the moneylender issues to you a receipt every time you make any repayment towards your loan, and check it for correctness (e.g. name, amount, date).
Make sure you receive a statement of account for all your subsisting loan(s) at least once every January and July, and check it for correctness (e.g. name, amount, date); and
You should retain all statement of accounts and receipts of payments, as documentation and evidence of payments.

questions.title: How do I make a complaint about a moneylender?
questions.text:
If you wish to complain about a moneylender for any reason, including unfair practices, contract issues, or potential offences, you may lodge a report with the Registry of Moneylenders or contact the Registry at 1800-2255-529*. When lodging a complaint, please keep in mind the following points:
(a) Provide all relevant documentary evidence to substantiate your complaint related to your loan transactions and circumstances of your dealings with the moneylender. Our officers may contact you for additional information or documents, or to schedule an interview.
(b) The Registry takes all complaints against moneylenders seriously and will investigate them thoroughly. Errant moneylenders will be taken to task.
(c) If a moneylender has engaged in an unfair practice towards you, you may consider pursuing the matter in Court under the Consumer Protection (Fair Trading) Act. The Court has the power to set aside loan transactions that are exorbitant or substantially unfair, depending on the Court's finding.
(d) If a moneylender has harassed you during the debt collection process, please lodge a police report in addition to informing the Registry.
Rest assured that the Registry will not disclose your details to the licensed moneylender without your consent.
*When calling the MinLaw Enquiry Line using the 1800 2255 529, please note that airtime charges may apply to calls made from mobile phones

questions.title: Are moneylenders allowed to collect payment from me at my place of residence or employment?
questions.text:
Licensed moneylenders can take reasonable steps to recover their debts as long as they do not infringe the law. Such steps may include contacting the borrower to ask for repayment and taking legal action to enforce the loan contract.
Approaching a debtor at his place of residence or employment to collect debts, while potentially embarrassing, does not necessarily constitute an offence. However, debt collectors cannot resort to vandalism, violence, or threatening words or behaviour, as such acts may infringe general criminal law. Whether or not a debt collection activity constitutes a criminal offence would depend on the facts of each case.
If there is any harassment, threat or violence involved in the course of debt recovery, you should lodge a police report, detailing your encounter(s) with them.

questions.title: Can I ban a family member from taking loans from all moneylenders?
questions.text:
The Registry of Moneylenders is not in a position to compel licensed moneylenders to not grant loans to a person who is otherwise eligible to be granted a loan legally. It is primarily the business decision of the licensed moneylender to determine if the loan should be granted, the suitable loan quantum if the loan is to be granted and the terms of the loan contract, etc.
The most effective solution to financial/debt management is for individuals to spend within their means. If a person needs to borrow, he should do so responsibly and take into consideration his ability to service and pay off outstanding loans without default.
An individual may apply for self-exclusion via the Moneylenders Credit Bureau ("MLCB"). Once the self-exclusion is registered, licensed moneylenders are not allowed to grant any unsecured loan (except a debt consolidation loan) to that individual. The self-exclusion period lasts for either 1 or 2 years¹ in which the individual is generally not allowed to withdraw from exclusion. On expiry of the minimum period, the self-exclusion remains in force until such time the individual withdraws from it.
The process is voluntary, and no individual may be excluded without his/ her consent.
¹Singapore Citizens/PRs may choose a minimum period of either 1 or 2 years. Foreigners need to fulfil a default minimum period of 2 years.

questions.title: What should I do if I receive SMS from moneylenders?
questions.text:
Licensed moneylenders are not allowed to advertise via SMS. Therefore, any SMS soliciting for loans, is either sent by a licensed moneylender in contravention of the advertising restrictions, or by an unlicensed moneylender.
Such unsolicited SMSes or calls from unknown sources which are related to loans or financial assistance are likely to be associated with unlicensed moneylending, which is a criminal offence. Do not respond to such advertisements.
If you receive such messages, please provide the information to Singapore Police Force through their online portal I-Witness.
If you suspect the SMS is sent by a licensed moneylender, you may write in to the Registry of Moneylenders via our Contact Us @ OneMinLaw with a screenshot of the SMS you received.

questions.title: How do I apply for a waiver certificate from the Pawnbrokers Act 2015?
questions.text:
Under section 43(1)(a) of the Pawnbrokers Act 2015, a company or other business entity may be granted a waiver from complying with the provisions of the Pawnbrokers Act 2015. There is no prescribed form for the application of a waiver certificate. Applicants are to write to the Registry with the following information and supporting documents:
i) A brief description of the applicant;
ii) A copy of the Instant Information Service printout on the applicant issued by ACRA;
iii) The business(es) and registered address(es) of the applicant;
iv) The telephone number(s) and email address(es) of the applicant;
v) A detailed description of each type of activity for which the waiver certificate is sought, including the specific goods involved, proposed processes, and the reasons for seeking a waiver;
vi) A detailed description of the types or classes of pawners in relation to each type of pawnbroking activity for which waiver is sought; and
vii) A draft scope of waiver for our consideration.
Applications may be submitted to the Registry via the following channels:
a) Mail to:

questions.title: When are the pawnbrokers' auctions?
questions.text:
With the enactment of the Pawnbrokers Act 2015 on 1 April 2015, pledges taken in by pawnbrokers from 1 April 2015 onwards that remain unredeemed on the expiry of the lawful redemption period will be forfeited instead of auctioned. In the event of such a forfeiture, the unredeemed pledges becomes the absolute property of the pawnbroker.
The last public auction of pawnbrokers' unredeemed pledges was held on 24 October 2015.
