For more information about DRS, visit https://io.mlaw.gov.sg/debt-repayment-scheme/about-debt-repayment-scheme/

questions.title: Why is there no breakdown of the deceased member’s CPF balances in the Deceased CPF Member Dashboard?
questions.text:
You can view the overall amount left in the deceased member’s CPF account under “Outstanding CPF balance”. This shows the combined total of all monies across the deceased member’s CPF accounts.
You may click on "View Transactions" to see a more detailed transaction history of the deceased's CPF accounts.

questions.title: I am an employee and/or platform worker, while also earning income as a self-employed person (SEP). How much Workfare Income Supplement will I receive in the same year?
questions.text:
You are considered a dual or multi status worker if you have more than one work status in the same year (employee, platform worker, self-employed person).
There are two parts to the Workfare Income Supplement (WIS) payment:
Monthly payments: Based on your employee and/or platform worker income if you meet the eligibility criteria.
Additional payment: After you declare your self-employment income (if any) and contribute the required MediSave in full, we’ll assess your eligibility.
You may receive additional WIS if your average monthly combined income qualifies for a higher WIS amount than what you already received and does not exceed the $3,000 threshold per month.
How much you receive will depend on your total income across all work types. Please refer to this FAQ for the maximum WIS amounts.
topics: Growing Your Savings / Workfare Income Supplement Scheme

questions.title: How can I access my next-of-kin's CPF account information if I cannot obtain their legal authorisation to receive it?
questions.text:
The Board, as a trustee of CPF monies belonging to CPF account holders, has a legal duty to maintain the confidentiality of their account information.
CPF Board will release account details — such as transaction history or a Yearly Statement of Account — only if one of the following applies:
The CPF member makes the request themselves
You have a Court Order authorising you to receive the information
You hold an activated Lasting Power of Attorney that covers this
topics: General Information & Useful Tips / Statement of account

questions.title: I am the primary caregiver for my next-of-kin. How do I request Transaction History on their behalf?
questions.text:
There are three ways to help your next-of-kin to access their Transaction History as their primary caregiver:
Option 1: Next-of-kin accesses Transaction History via Singpass
Your next-of-kin can log in with Singpass on the CPF Mobile app or my cpf digital services to view, save or download their Transaction History. Please refer to this FAQ for a step-by-step guide.
If your next-of-kin does not have a Singpass, they can visit the Singpass website to obtain one.
Option 2: Caregiver assistance through Singpass Multi-User SMS 2FA
If your next-of-kin needs help with government digital services, they can set you up as a trusted caregiver through the Singpass Multi-User SMS 2FA. This is a one-time setup, which allows you to help your next-of-kin access their CPF account information online more conveniently in future.
Please refer to Singpass FAQs for more information on Multi-User SMS 2FA.
Option 3: Appointed donee/deputy
If you are the appointed donee/deputy for your next-of-kin under the Mental Capacity Act, you can access their CPF information directly using Singpass Multi-User SMS 2FA.
Please refer to this FAQ for the process and required documents.
If you are unable to access your next-of-kin’s Transaction History through the options above, please refer to this FAQ for more information.
topics: General Information & Useful Tips / Statement of account

questions.title: Who can commence an action in the Employment Claims Tribunals?
questions.text:
Only Employees and Employers can commence an action in the Employment Claims Tribunals.
For more information, you may visit https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/file-employment-claim .
topics: Employment Claims Tribunals / Commencing an Employment Claim: General Information

questions.title: Can a lawyer represent me in an Employment Claims Tribunals matter?
questions.text:
No, you must present your own case and cannot engage a lawyer to represent you in Employment Claims Tribunals matters. If you are an employer, and your business is incorporated as a company or operates as a partnership, you may be represented by an officer or a full-time employee.
For more information on representation in the ECT, please head to the following link: https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/before-going-to-court-employment-claim.
topics: Employment Claims Tribunals / Commencing an Employment Claim: General Information

questions.title: Is mediation compulsory before I am able commence a claim at the Employment Claims Tribunals?
questions.text:
Mediation at the Tripartite Alliance for Dispute Management (TADM) is compulsory before claims can be filed at the Employment Claims Tribunals (ECT).
Additionally, you may only file a claim at the ECT if both of the following applies:
(a) Your dispute is unresolved after mediation at TADM.
(b) You have been issued a Claim Referral Certificate by an approved TADM mediator.
If you have yet to file a mediation request, you may do so at this link: https://www.tal.sg/tadm/eservices
topics: Employment Claims Tribunals / Commencing an Employment Claim: Prerequisities

questions.title: What are the criteria I must meet before I can file a claim at the Employment Claims Tribunals?
questions.text:
You must meet all of the following criteria before you are eligible to file a claim at the Employment Claims Tribunals:
Mediation Efforts
1. Your dispute remains unresolved after mediation at the Tripartite Alliance for Dispute Management (TADM) and you have been issued a Claim Referral Certificate by the TADM mediator.
Claim Limit
2. Your claim must not exceed $20,000. Where you have undergone the Tripartite Mediation Framework or mediations assisted by unions recognised under the Industrial Relations Act, your claim can go beyond $20,000 but must not exceed $30,000.
Type of Claim
3. (i) You are an employee who has either a Statutory salary-related claim, Contractual salary-related claim, or Wrongful dismissal claim. To find out if your claim falls under the scope of the aforementioned claims, please click on the links below.
OR
3. (ii) You are an employer who has a salary in lieu of notice of termination claim.
View the types of claims available here: https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/cases-eligible-employment-claim#types-claims
Registered Country/Citizenship
4. You are claiming against a party who is residing, or has a registered office or place of business, in Singapore.

questions.title: When must I file an Employment Claim by?
questions.text:
You must file an Employment Claim within 4 weeks after obtaining the Claim Referral Certificate from Tripartite Alliance for Dispute Management (TADM).
For more information, you may visit https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/how-to-file-serve-employment-claim .
topics: Employment Claims Tribunals / Commencing an Employment Claim: Filing

questions.title: What are the list of documents I need in order to file an Employment Claim?
questions.text:
You should prepare a soft copy of the following in PDF format (where applicable) before you file:
1. Your personal identification documents.
2. (For Singapore citizens or permanent residents) National Registration Identity Card (NRIC) or passport, (For foreign citizens) Passport and employment pass, (For company representatives) Latest ACRA profile, letter of authorisation and NRIC, passport or employment pass of representative.
3. The Claim Referral Certificate from Tripartite Alliance for Dispute Management (TADM) and the latest ACRA Profile of the employer.
4. Other supporting documents for the claim (for example, employment contract pay slips, written record of key employment terms, time sheets or bank statements).
5. The particulars of the respondent.
6. You will need to provide the name, personal identification number and address of the respondent.
All supporting documents submitted must be in the English language. Otherwise, a certified translation for the documents must be provided.
For more information, you may visit https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/how-to-file-serve-employment-claim - where the list of documents is listed under the "What you will need" section.
topics: Employment Claims Tribunals / Commencing an Employment Claim: Filing

questions.title: Can I make a joint claim with other parties against the same respondent?
questions.text: No, multiple parties cannot make joint claims against one respondent.
topics: Employment Claims Tribunals / Commencing an Employment Claim: Filing

questions.title: Can I file two or more claims together?
questions.text: Yes, provided that you are not filing a salary-related claim and a wrongful dismissal claim together. These two claims cannot be jointly filed.
topics: Employment Claims Tribunals / Commencing an Employment Claim: Filing

questions.title: What must I do after I have filed my Employment Claim?
questions.text:
You must now serve the Notice of Case Management Conference (CMC) on the Respondent. This must be done so within 7 days of the date of filing of the Claim. After that, you must file a Declaration of Service within 4 weeks of the date of filing of the claim or before the date of the first CMC, whichever is earlier.
For more information, you may visit https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/how-to-file-serve-employment-claim - under the "How to file and serve" section.
topics: Employment Claims Tribunals / Commencing an Employment Claim: Service

questions.title: What is Service? / What does Service mean?
questions.text:
"Service" refers to the delivering of the document to the Respondent. This can be done by Personal Service (delivering hard copies of the document physically to the Respondent), by Registered Post to their last known residential or registered address or ACRA registered address (for businesses), or by any other means as directed by the ECT.
For more information, you may visit https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/how-to-file-serve-employment-claim - under the "How to file and serve" section.
topics: Employment Claims Tribunals / Commencing an Employment Claim: Service

questions.title: What do I, as a Claimant, need to serve on the Respondent?
questions.text:
You must serve on the Respondent a copy of the Claim Form, the Notice of Case Management Conference, as well as every document on which you rely or will rely, and the reports on the findings of the approved mediator, an authorised person, the Commissioner, or an inspector referred to in rule 8(3)(b) of the Employment Claims Rules 2017 (if any).
For more information, you may visit https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/how-to-file-serve-employment-claim - under the "How to file and serve" section.
topics: Employment Claims Tribunals / Commencing an Employment Claim: Service

questions.title: What must I do after I have served the Respondent?
questions.text:
You must file a Declaration of Service within 4 weeks of the date of filing of the claim or before the date of the first Case Management Conference, whichever is earlier.
For more information, you may visit https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/how-to-file-serve-employment-claim - under the "How to file and serve" section.
topics: Employment Claims Tribunals / Commencing an Employment Claim: Service

questions.title: I received a Notice of Case Management Conference which someone sent to me. What do I do now?
questions.text:
This means an Employment Claim has been commenced against you.
You should now:
1. Log in to Community Justice and Tribunals System to view the details of the claim made against you.
2. Understand the process of responding to an employment claim.
3. Understand the orders the Employment Claims Tribunals can make.
After you have done all of the above, you may now respond to the claim against you. You have 3 ways to do so:
1. Settle the claim — you and the claimant come to an agreement on the dispute.
2. Dispute the claim — you want to contest the claimant's case against you in Court.
3. File a counterclaim — you want to contest the claimant's case against you in Court and commence a case against the Claimant. Take note, however, that a counterclaim may only be filed after you and the claimant have first gone through mediation at the Tripartite Alliance for Dispute Management.
Click this link for a more elaborate explanation on the different processes: https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/how-to-respond-employment-claim
topics: Employment Claims Tribunals / Responding to an Employment Claim

questions.title: What is a Case Management Conference (CMC)?
questions.text:
A CMC is a session in which a registrar will manage the case and give the parties an opportunity to resolve their dispute beyond the opportunity they would have had at the mediation conducted by the Tripartite Alliance for Dispute Management. If the parties are able to reach a settlement for all or some of the matters in dispute during the CMC, the parties can either enter a settlement agreement or make a request to the registrar for the agreement to be recorded as a consent order.
If the parties are unable to settle some or all of their dispute at the CMC, the registrar will give directions on how the case should proceed. This would typically including directions for the parties to file the evidence they wish to rely on, and fixing a hearing date for parties to appear before a tribunal magistrate to make a determination on the case. It is mandatory for both the Claimant and Respondent to attend the CMC.
For more information about what to expect at a CMC, you may visit https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/at-employment-claims-CMC

questions.title: What if I don’t attend the a Case Management Conference (CMC)?
questions.text:
If you are absent from a CMC without any reasonable excuse, the registrar may continue with the proceedings and make a default order against you. There are two types of default orders which can be made in this case: If you are the Claimant who fails to attend court, a default dismissal order may be made against you. This means that your claim has been dismissed.
If you are the Respondent who fails to attend court, a default money order may be made in favour of the Claimant. This means you will have to pay the Claimant the sum of money stated in the order by the due date, failing which the Claimant may start enforcement proceedings against you.
If you were absent from a CMC an a default order has been entered against you, and you intend to apply to set that order aside, visit this link for more information about setting aside: https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/set-aside-employment-claims-order-made-in-absence

questions.title: What if I can't make it for my Case Management Conference (CMC)?
questions.text:
You may request a change of court date (which is subject to approval). Such request may be made by filing a "Change of Court Date Application" on the Community Justice and Tribunals System (CJTS). Before filing a Change of Court Date Application on CJTS, however, you should start by seeking the written consent of the other party.
If the other party consents to a change of date, you should then obtain (in writing) the other party's unavailable dates and times for at least 3 weeks following the scheduled date for your CMC. You should also identify your own unavailable dates and times. These dates and times will allow the Tribunal to reschedule the CMC to a date on which both parties are available.
Once you have proof of the other party's consent and their unavailable dates and times, you may proceed to file your Change of Court Date Application. In this application, you should: (1) explain why you are unavailable and attach proof of your unavailability (if any); (2) state that you have obtained the other party's consent for the CMC to be rescheduled and attach proof of the other party's consent; and (3) state both yours and the other party's unavailable dates and times as well as proof of the other party's unavailability.
If, however, the other party does not consent to a change of date and you wish to proceed with a Change of Court Date Application, you should inform the other party of your intention. You may then proceed to file your Change of Court Date Application. In this application, you should: (1) explain why you are unavailable and attach proof of your unavailability (if any); (2) state that you have sought the other party's consent but that they have not given it, and attach proof of your communications with the other party; and (3) state your unavailable dates.
In whichever case, you should take steps to file a Change of Court Date Application as early as possible.

questions.title: How do I set aside a default order made against me?
questions.text:
You must file an application on CJTS to set aside the order within 7 days after the default order was made. Subsequently, you will need to serve the Notice of Application and the Notice of Hearing to Set Aside on the Respondent.
For more information on how to set aside a default order entered against you, you may visit this link: https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/set-aside-employment-claims-order-made-in-absence

questions.title: What if I intend to dispute the other party's application to set aside a default order made against them?
questions.text: You must file and serve a Response to the setting aside application on the Applicant (ie, the other party who seeking to set aside the default order made against them) within 7 days after he has served the Notice of Application and Notice of Hearing to Set Aside on you. This can be done through the General Applications tab on CJTS.

questions.title: If I can't be represented by a lawyer in Employment Claims Tribunals (ECT) proceedings, can I be represented by another person?
questions.text:
Generally, parties must present their own cases in the ECT. However, you may be represented by another person in specific circumstances.
For more details about those specific circumstances and who may represent you if those circumstances are met, please visit this link: https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/before-going-to-court-employment-claim.
If you meet the requirements to be represented by another person, you may file an "Application for Representative" on the Community Justice and Tribunals System to seek the ECT's approval.
In this application, you should: (1) state clearly the specific circumstances you are relying on; (2) submit proof of those circumstances; (3) state the identity of the proposed representative and how he or she is related to you; and (4) submit a letter authorising the proposed representative to act as your representative in the proceedings before the ECT.

questions.title: Can another person / party accompany me to ECT proceedings?
questions.text:
Yes, parties may be accompanied by a family member, friend or volunteer under the CCT Friend Scheme. This request is subject to the ECT's approval.
You may visit this link for more information: https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/legal-help-support/cct-friend-scheme

questions.title: What is a "Hearing" before a tribunal magistrate of the Employment Claims Tribunals?
questions.text:
A hearing is a session in which a tribunal magistrate will hear the parties' cases and make a determination on the dispute. During the hearing, both the Claimant and Respondent will have the opportunity to present their evidence and arguments.
The hearing is conducted informally, and the tribunal magistrate will adopt a judge-led approach – identifying the relevant issues and ensuring that the relevant evidence is adduced by the parties. The tribunal magistrate is not bound by the rules of evidence and may inquire into any matter which the tribunal magistrate considers relevant to the claim. After considering all the evidence and submissions, the tribunal magistrate will make an order to resolve the dispute. This may include orders for the payment of money, the dismissal of the claim, the payment of costs, or (in wrongful dismissal cases) reinstatement.
A full list of potential orders which the tribunal can make is found here: https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/at-employment-claims-hearing. It is mandatory for both the Claimant and Respondent to attend the hearing.
For more information about what to expect at an ECT hearing, please click this link: https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/at-employment-claims-hearing

questions.title: What if a party does not comply with the Employment Claims Tribunals (ECT) Order made against him?
questions.text:
The other party may commence enforcement proceedings against that party. An order made by a tribunal may be enforced in the same manner as a judgment given or an order made by a District Court. If you do not know the assets which the other party has, you may file an application for an Order for Examination of Enforcement Respondent. This allows you to question the other party on oath about their assets, income, and financial circumstances, so that you can decide on the most appropriate method of enforcement. Once you know what assets the other party has, you may file a Single Application for Enforcement to enforce the order.
The types of enforcement orders you may apply for include the following:
Writ of Seizure and Sale: This allows the Court bailiff to seize and sell the other party's movable property (such as goods, vehicles, or shares) or immovable property (such as land or a house) to satisfy the judgment debt.
Garnishee Order: This allows you to recover the judgment debt from a third party who owes money to, or holds money on behalf of, the other party. For example, if the other party has money in a bank account, you may apply for a garnishee order against the bank.
Charging Order: This imposes a charge on the other party's interest in property (such as land, securities, or funds in court), which may prevent the other party from disposing of that property without satisfying the judgment debt.
Appointment of Receiver: This allows the Court to appoint a receiver to collect income or assets on behalf of the judgment creditor.
Order for Delivery/Recovery of Movable Property: This allows you to recover specific movable property from the other party.
Order for Possession of Immovable Property: This allows you to recover possession of land or premises from the other party.
The guides on how to file the above may be found below:
How to file a Single Application for Enforcement: https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/single-enforcement-application
How to file an Order for Examination of Enforcement Respondent: https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/civil-claims-(from-1-april-2022)/enforce-an-order-or-judgment-(from-1-april-2022)/examination-of-enforcement-respondent-(from-1-april-2022)/file-an-order-for-examination-of-enforcement-respondent-(from-1-april-2022)

questions.title: What if I am not satisfied with an Order made by a registrar?
questions.text:
If you are dissatisfied with a decision, direction, or order made by the Registrar (for example, at a Case Management Conference), you may appeal to a tribunal. You may do so by filing an "Appeal Against Order of Registrar" on the Community Justice and Tribunals System (CJTS) and paying the applicable fee.
You must file the appeal on CJTS within 7 days after the decision, direction, or order was made, and serve it on all other parties within 7 days after filing. Note that filing an appeal does not automatically stop the proceedings from continuing. If you wish the proceedings to be stayed while the appeal is pending, you will need to ask the tribunal or Registrar to make an order to that effect.
For more information on appeals against the decisions, directions, or order made by the Registrar, you may visit: https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/appeal-employment-claims-order-registrar

questions.title: What if I am not satisfied with an Order made by a tribunal magistrate?
questions.text:
If you are dissatisfied with an order made by a tribunal magistrate at a hearing, you may appeal to the General Division of the High Court. However, you can only appeal on a ground involving a question of law, or on the ground that the claim was outside the jurisdiction of the tribunal. Before you can appeal, you must first obtain permission from a District Court. You may do so by filing an "Application for Leave/Permission to Appeal" on the Community Justice and Tribunals System (CJTS) and paying the applicable fee. You must file the application on CJTS within 7 days after the date of the order, and serve it on the other party within 7 days after filing. If the other party intends to oppose your application, they must file and serve a response within 7 days after being served. If the District Court grants permission, you must then file and serve a notice of appeal within 7 days after permission is given.
At the time of filing, you must also provide security for the other party's costs of appeal in the sum of $500. Note that filing an appeal does not automatically stop the order from being enforced. If you wish to stop enforcement while the appeal is pending, you will need to apply to a District Court or the General Division of the High Court for a stay. In hearing the appeal, the General Division of the High Court may dismiss the appeal, allow the appeal and set aside or vary the order, or send the matter back to the tribunal for reconsideration. However, the High Court cannot overturn any finding of fact made by the tribunal, and cannot consider any new evidence. The decision of the High Court is final.
For more information on appeals against orders made by tribunal magistrates, you may visit: https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/appeal-employment-claims-order-tribunal

questions.title: Why are platform workers who have not opted in to the increased CPF contributions ineligible to receive Workfare Income Supplement aligned to that of employees from 2029?
questions.text: Platform workers who have not opted in to increased CPF contributions will continue to contribute to their Medisave Account only, like self-employed persons (SEPs). Thus, the Workfare Income Supplement for these eligible platform workers are aligned with SEPs.
topics: Growing Your Savings / Workfare Income Supplement Scheme

questions.title: How will the monthly per capita household income be determined for assessing one's eligibility for the Silver Support Scheme?
questions.text:
The monthly per capita household income is calculated by dividing the total gross household monthly income by the total number of family members living together. Gross monthly household income includes basic employment income, trade/self-employed income, overtime pay, allowances, cash awards, commissions, and bonuses.
The monthly income of each member will be determined based on the following:
Salaried Employees:
1. Monthly income as declared to CPF Board by the member’s employer(s), averaged over 12 months; or
2. The latest available annual income assessment by the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) within the last two calendar years.
Self-Employed Persons:
1. Monthly income as declared to CPF Board by the member as a self-employed person, averaged over 12 months; or
2. The latest available annual income assessment by the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) within the last two calendar years.
Platform Workers:
1. Monthly income as declared to CPF Board by the member’s platform operator(s), averaged over 12 months; or
2. The latest available annual income assessment by the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) within the last two calendar years.
If there have been recent changes to your circumstances that may affect your eligibility, please write to us for a reassessment and we will work with the HOusehold Means Eligibility System (HOMES) team to have your household means tested.

questions.title: How can I change my mode of payment to receive cash benefits from the Government?
questions.text:
There are two options to update the mode of payment for your government cash benefits:
Option 1: Link your NRIC to PayNow
You are encouraged to link your NRIC to PayNow as government cash benefits will be credited to your PayNow-NRIC-linked bank account. To find out more on how to link your NRIC to PayNow, please refer to this FAQ.
If your NRIC is linked to your PayNow, there is no need for you to provide your bank account details.
Option 2: Provide your bank account details
You can submit your bank account details by logging in to our e-services with your Singpass. The bank account that you provide will only be used if you do not have a PayNow-NRIC linked bank account.
Bank crediting is available only via the three local banking groups DBS/POSB, OCBC, UOB, and your bank account must be a personal or joint account linked to your NRIC number.
The Government will verify the bank account details you have registered with your bank. If you have closed your bank account, ceased being a joint account holder, or provided incorrect bank account details, you will be asked to update your bank account details. A letter will be sent to your NRIC address.
No further action is required if you have already linked your NRIC to PayNow with a participating bank.

questions.title: What can I do if the person who lost their IC is unable to report the loss online or in person?
questions.text:
The IC holder should report the loss of IC himself/herself as IC is a personal document.
However, you may report the loss of IC on behalf of the holder via FormSG if the holder is unable to report the loss of IC himself/herself due to medical reasons.
In your submission, you are required to attach the following documents:
A medical memo from a doctor outlining the individual's medical condition
A completed copy of the “Application for replacement of NRIC (loss)” form
A court order or Lasting Power of Attorney (LPA) appointing you as a donee (if the individual is assessed to be mentally incapacitated to make decisions), or a court-appointed deputyship
We will review your application and reach out to you once we have completed our review.

questions.title: How is the Annual Value (AV) requirement for Workfare Income Supplement scheme determined and which address is used to calculate it?
questions.text:
The Annual Value (AV) threshold for Workfare Income Supplement (WIS) covers all HDB flats and some smaller private residences. In general, Singaporeans staying in larger properties with an AV above the threshold tend to have greater access to household wealth, making them ineligible for WIS.
The AV of a property is the estimated market rental of similar properties in the area, as determined by IRAS.
To assess your WIS eligibility, we use your NRIC address to check the AV of your place of residence. For accurate assessment, please ensure your NRIC reflects your current place of residence.
Under the National Registration Act, you are required to report any change of address within 28 days at the Immigration & Checkpoints Authority (ICA) website.
topics: Growing Your Savings / Workfare Income Supplement Scheme

questions.title: Why is my spouse's Assessable Income for the previous Year of Assessment used to determine my Workfare Income Supplement in the current work year?
questions.text:
This is to allow for quicker assessment of Workfare Income Supplement (WIS) eligibility. As Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) needs time to process Income data for the current work year, we use the latest Assessable Income (AI) data to determine eligibility.
The AI for the previous Year of Assessment (YOA) is used to assess one's WIS eligibility for the current year. For example, we will use your spouse's AI for YOA 2025 to assess your eligibility for 2026 WIS.
topics: Growing Your Savings / Workfare Income Supplement Scheme

questions.title: Why will the Workfare Income Supplement for platform workers be aligned with that of employees only in 2029, when their increased CPF contributions were implemented in 2025?
questions.text:
CPF contributions rates for platform workers will gradually increase from 2025 to 2028, and will fully align with those of employees in 2029. Correspondingly, the Workfare Income Supplement will be aligned with employee rates only from 2029, for platform workers who are mandated or have opted in to the increased CPF contributions.
During this period, the Platform Workers CPF Transition Support (PCTS) will provide monthly cash payments to support lower-income platform workers who make increased CPF contributions. The PCTS will fully cover the increase in CPF contributions in 2025 and will gradually taper off before ending in 2029.
topics: Growing Your Savings / Workfare Income Supplement Scheme

questions.title: Why is my Workfare Income Supplement amount different from previous months?
questions.text:
For employees and platform workers, your Workfare Income Supplement (WIS) amount may differ monthly as it depends on your income. It is assessed monthly based on your total gross income as declared by your employer or platform operator in the CPF submissions. If you have more than one source of income, income from all sources will be considered. Any change in your total income can result in a different WIS payment.
You can use the online WIS calculator to estimate your payment.
topics: Growing Your Savings / Workfare Income Supplement Scheme

questions.title: When will I get my Workfare Income Supplement payment?
questions.text:
This depends on your employment type.
For an employee and/or platform worker1,2
We usually pay your Workfare Income Supplement (WIS) two months after the month you worked. You will receive WIS for every month you work.
If you worked inYou will receive the WIS in your bank account or via GovCash
PayNow-NRIC / Bank CreditingGovCash
JanEnd Mar1st week of April
FebEnd Apr1st week of May
MarEnd May1st week of June

You can log in to our e-services with your Singpass to check your payment details after the payment has been made to your bank account or via GovCash.
For a self-employed person (SEP)
You will get WIS payment yearly for work done in the previous Work Year (WY).
To get the earliest payment by end April of the following WY (WY + 1), you need to complete these by 31 March of the following year (WY + 1):
Declare your net trade income (NTI) to IRAS
Make your corresponding MediSave contributions in full based on your declared NTI earned in the WY without accounting for previous years’ losses
If you declare your income and make your MediSave contributions after 31 March of the following year (WY + 1), you will get your WIS within two months after you complete making your MediSave contributions.
1For Work Year 2024 and earlier, platform workers receive WIS as SEPs. Please refer to the 'WIS for self-employed persons' for more information.
2If you have also worked as a SEP in the same work year, you may get additional WIS as a dual status worker.
topics: Growing Your Savings / Workfare Income Supplement Scheme

questions.title: What if I prefer not to receive payments via GovCash?
questions.text:
If you prefer not to receive your payments via Govcash, there are two options available:
Option 1: Link your NRIC to PayNow with a participating bank
We encourage you to link your NRIC to PayNow with a participating PayNow-GIRO bank.
The list of PayNow-GIRO-participating banks are: Bank of China, CIMB, Citibank, DBS Bank / POSB, GXS Bank, HL Bank, HSBC Bank, ICBC, MariBank, Maybank, OCBC Bank, RHB Bank, Standard Chartered Bank, State Bank of India, Trust Bank and UOB Bank.
If your preferred bank is on this list, contact your bank for details on how to link your NRIC to PayNow.
Once you link your NRIC to PayNow, future Government benefits you are eligible for will be automatically credited to your PayNow-linked bank account.
Option 2: Register your bank account details
Alternatively, you can choose to receive your payments via crediting to your bank account. To do so, log in to the e-services using your Singpass, select “Bank Account Submission” and update your POSB/DBS, OCBC or UOB bank account details.
Bank crediting is available only via the three local banking groups DBS/POSB, OCBC, UOB, and your bank account must be a personal or joint account registered with your NRIC number.
The Government will verify the bank account details you have registered with your bank. If you have closed your bank account, ceased being a joint account holder, or have provided incorrect bank account details, you will be asked to update your bank account details. A letter will be sent to your NRIC address.
topics: Growing Your Savings / Workfare Income Supplement Scheme

questions.title: Why is monthly per capita household income used as an indication of my family support for the Silver Support Scheme?
questions.text:
The Silver Support (SS) Scheme is targeted at seniors who had low incomes during their working years and now have little or no family support and resources in their retirement.
To automatically identify seniors who are eligible for SS, the Government has to rely on available data as broad indicators of an individual’s ability to save for retirement, access to resources and family support.
We have relied on the monthly per capita household income as a broad indicator of the level of family support available.

questions.title: Can I use CPF savings for my full-time subsidised local degree course if I have previously used CPF savings for my first subsidised diploma course?
questions.text: You can use CPF savings for your degree course as long as it is an approved full-time subsidised course under the CPF Education Loan Scheme, subject to the available withdrawal limit.
topics: Other Schemes / CPF Education Loan Scheme

questions.title: What is the SGSHARE Programme?
questions.text:
SGSHARE is the national regular-giving programme that supports communities in need. It is an initiative by Community Chest, the philanthropic arm of the National Council of Social Service, to provide sustained funding for programmes and capability-building for social service agencies serving communities in need.
The CPF Board collects your employees’ SGSHARE donations on behalf of Community Chest, from the employees’ wages made through the company payroll.

questions.title: How do I pay my employees' SGSHARE donations?
questions.text: You are expected to deduct the SGSHARE donations from your employees’ wages and pay the SGSHARE donations together with the CPF contributions.

questions.title: My employees do not wish to contribute to the SGSHARE programme. What can they do?
questions.text: Your employees can contact the HR department to cease the payroll deduction if they do not wish to contribute to SGSHARE programme.

questions.title: Can I use my MediSave to pay for dental treatments?
questions.text:
You can use your MediSave for selected complex dental procedures that involve surgery and are performed for medical reasons, subject to the MediSave withdrawal limits applicable for day surgeries.
If you are aged 60 or older, you can also use your available withdrawal limit under Flexi-MediSave for selected non-surgical dental procedures such as permanent crowns and root canal treatments.
Please check with your dentist whether your dental treatments are MediSave-claimable.

questions.title: Can I use MediSave to pay the MediShield Life deductible for outpatient treatment?
questions.text: Yes, you can use your MediSave to pay for your MediShield Life outpatient deductible. There is also MediFund to help those who are unable to afford their bills even after subsidies, MediShield Life, and MediSave. Nobody will be denied appropriate care due to an inability to pay.

questions.title: I was told by my dentist that Flexi-MediSave does not cover all dental treatments. Why is that so?
questions.text:
Flexi-MediSave is meant to help with recurrent outpatient medical expenses, which many older Singaporeans have raised as a key concern due to significant accumulated bill sizes over the longer term.
Flexi-MediSave can be used for select restorative dental procedures, i.e. permanent crowns and root canal treatments which can be relatively more costly. Other dental expenses are not covered under Flexi-MediSave and patients can benefit from generous government subsidies to cover costs – for example, at CHAS dental clinics and public institutions such as the polyclinics and National Dental Centre.
Nevertheless, you can use MediSave under the MediSave withdrawal limits applicable for day surgeries for selected complex dental procedures.

questions.title: I can't find my Year-in-Review. How do I access it?
questions.text:
As part of our ongoing efforts to improve our services and better engage our members, we have heard your feedback for more forward-planning tools and have recently launched PLAN with CPF – your one-stop financial guidance platform that helps you make informed financial decisions as you navigate through life. We have discontinued the Year-in-Review pilot from June 2026.
You may continue to view your annual CPF balances, inflow and outflow using the Yearly Statement of Account (YSOA) or check Transaction history for recent activities.
topics: General Information & Useful Tips / Statement of account

questions.title: Why is making MediSave contributions important for self-employed persons?
questions.text:
As a self-employed person, it is important to set aside a portion of your income to build up your MediSave savings. These savings can be used for your healthcare needs such as MediShield Life premiums or hospitalisation costs, helping to safeguard your healthcare expenses especially when you are older or no longer working.
If you are having difficulties making your MediSave contributions, you can request an instalment plan1 for your MediSave contributions via the Manage your MediSave payable form.
1Please note that your request is subject to the Board’s approval. You may be required to provide additional information or supporting documents, if necessary.

questions.title: Why do I need to make MediSave contributions as a self-employed person?
questions.text:
You are required to make mandatory MediSave contributions as a self-employed person if you earn a total net trade income of more than $6,000.
These MediSave contributions helps you to build up savings for your healthcare needs, especially in the absence of regular MediSave contributions from an employer.

questions.title: I am unable to make my MediSave contributions in full. What should I do?
questions.text:
If you are having difficulties making your MediSave contributions in full, you can request an instalment plan1 for your MediSave contributions via the Manage your MediSave payable form. This allows you to make your contributions conveniently in more manageable monthly instalments, with automatic deductions from your bank account.
1Please note that your request is subject to the Board’s approval. You may be required to provide additional information or supporting documents, if necessary.

questions.title: Will a Singaporean Seaman be required to make CPF Contributions in respect of his employment?
questions.text:
It depends on when the Singaporean seaman started working onboard the vessel and whether he continues employment under the same employer from before 1 June 2026.
A Singaporean seaman will continue to remain exempt from CPF contributions on or after 1 June 2026 if he was already serving onboard a Norwegian, Swedish, or East Asiatic Co Ltd (EACL) vessel before 1 June 2026 under an existing employment contract. This exemption continues even if his contract is renewed, extended, or replaced by a new contract within 1 month of the previous contract's termination or expiry date (where the same applies for subsequent renewals/extensions/new contracts) with the same employer, or if he transfers to another Norwegian, Swedish, or EACL vessel under the same employer.
CPF contributions will be required if the seaman starts working onboard a Norwegian, Swedish or EACL vessel on or after 1 June 2026 under a new contract where he had not previously worked onboard any such Norwegian, Swedish or EACL vessel under the same employer prior to 1 June 2026. CPF contributions will also be required if the seaman joins a non-Norwegian, Swedish, or EACL vessel or changes employer.

questions.title: What are the operating hours for the Prison Link Centres?
questions.text:
The operating hours for the Prison Link Centres (PLCs):
Mondays to Fridays: 8am to 5pm
Saturdays: 8am to 4pm
Closed on Sundays and Public Holidays

questions.title: Can I bring in pets during visits?
questions.text:
Pets are not allowed during visits.
For more information, visit: https://www.sps.gov.sg/visit-matters/visit-information/how-to-visit/

questions.title: Are photocopies of the birth certificates accepted as proof of relationship during visits?
questions.text:
Please note that only original documents will be accepted.
Visitors can apply for a certified birth extract on behalf of the inmate via the ICA Website at https://www.ica.gov.sg/documents/birth/apply_extract

questions.title: What is the validity of the Visit Card?
questions.text: There is no expiry date for a Visit Card.

questions.title: My ex-spouse passed away. Can I submit the Beneficiary Representative claim for my child?
questions.text: If your child is below 21 years old, you will not be able to submit a Beneficiary Representative claim. Instead, you may submit a claim for your child, along with supporting documents to prove the relationship between your child and your ex-spouse. Your child’s share of the CPF monies will be held in trust by the Public Trustee (“PT”) until your child is 21 years old.

questions.title: In what circumstances will the beneficiaries’ share of the CPF moneys be held by the Public Trustee?
questions.text:
There are circumstances where beneficiaries’ share of the deceased’s un-nominated CPF monies will be held by the Public Trustee. This applies to beneficiaries who are:
Minors below 21 years old, whose entitlements will be held until they attain the age of 21.
Beneficiaries who are uncontactable, whose entitlements will be held by the Public Trustee until they submit a claim.
Prison inmates. They may approach the Public Trustee’s Office to receive their entitlements upon their release from prison.
Undischarged bankrupts who must have their entitlement paid to the Official Assignee or Private Trustee in Bankruptcy.
Beneficiaries who are mentally incapacitated and have appointed deputy(s). Their entitlements will be paid to the deputy(s) unless consent is given by the deputy for the Beneficiary Representative to receive the monies on his/her behalf.
All other beneficiaries not specified above will have their shares paid to the Beneficiary Representative if they have provided their consent.

questions.title: What if the Beneficiary Representative failed to disclose a beneficiary to Public Trustee and obtain that beneficiary’s consent?
questions.text:
The Public Trustee’s Office will take steps to verify the beneficiaries stated in the application based on available information and records. The Public Trustee’s Office will seek clarification from the Beneficiary Representative should there be a discrepancy between the information submitted and our records.
The onus is on the Beneficiary Representative to fully disclose the information of all the beneficiaries for the Public Trustee’s Office to ascertain their consent. In circumstances where the Beneficiary Representative failed to disclose a beneficiary (and no records of the beneficiary are observed in the Public Trustee’s records) and the latter comes forth to claim his / her entitlement of the CPF monies that has been paid to the Beneficiary Representative, the beneficiary will be directed to the Beneficiary Representative to resolve the matter in private. Actions may also be taken against the Beneficiary Representative for making a false declaration.

questions.title: I received a letter before the commencement of the Beneficiary Representative approach (18 June 2022) informing me of the deceased’s un-nominated CPF monies and to make an application. Can I choose to submit a Beneficiary Representative claim application?
questions.text: Yes, the Beneficiary Representative claim will apply for cases in which the un-nominated CPF monies were received by the Public Trustee before 18 June 2022, provided that the amount does not exceed $10,000.

questions.title: How much do I need to refund to my CPF account when selling/transferring my property?
questions.text:
To check the exact amount that you need to refund your CPF accounts if you sell/transfer your property, simply log in to your Home ownership dashboard and look under the “What Happens If” section.
In general, the amount you must refund is the principal you have withdrawn for your property (P) and the accrued interest (I), i.e. “P+I”. If you are age 55 or above and have pledged your property to set aside your retirement sum, you must also refund the pledged amount.
IMPORTANT NOTE:
However, please note that your required CPF refund is less than your P+I if you:
were age 55 or older before 1 January 2013; and
have set aside your Full Retirement Sum (FRS) before 1 January 2013.
This is because having set aside your FRS before 1 January 2013, you are not required by law to refund the CPF you have used to pay for your property prior to 2013. If you have continued to use your CPF from 1 January 2013, only the principal amount used from 1 January 2013 and the accrued interest need to be refunded when you sell your property.

questions.title: What can I do if I have not received my Cashier’s Order or my Cashier’s Order has expired?
questions.text:
We typically dispatch the Cashier's Order within five working days of completion of processing. Time taken for the Cashier’s Order to reach you will depend on your country’s postal services.
If you have not received your Cashier's Order within two months of submitting your online application form or your Cashier’s Order has expired, please contact the Board through Write to Us.
topics: Account Services / Account closure for non-Singapore Citizens and non-PRs

questions.title: Will a domestic employee be required to make CPF contributions in respect of his/her employment?
questions.text:
It depends on the domestic employee's working hours and whether he/she continues working for the same employer from before 1 June 2026.
If the domestic employee worked 14 hours or less per week (i.e. in any consecutive 7-day period) in all weeks of at least one calendar month before 1 June 2026, he/she will qualify for exemption from CPF contributions.
After qualifying, the exemption will continue to apply from 1 June 2026 onwards for each month that the domestic employee continues working for the same employer and does not work more than 14 hours in any consecutive 7-day period.
The exemption continues even if the contract is renewed, extended, or replaced by a new contract within 1 month of the previous contract's termination or expiry (where the same applies for subsequent renewals / extensions / new contracts). Changes to the job scope that relate exclusively to the household's domestic needs will not affect the exemption if the employee continues to satisfy the definition of domestic employee and continues working for the same employer.
CPF contributions will be required if the domestic employee works more than 14 hours in any consecutive 7-day period in a calendar month, enters into a contract with a new employer on or after 1 June 2026, changes his/her job scope to a non-domestic role, or enters into a subsequent contract with the same employer more than 1 month after the previous contract's termination or expiry.

questions.title: How do I update my new address with Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) if I have moved?
questions.text:
If there is a change in your address, please update your new address with Immigration & Checkpoints Authority (ICA) online using this [link]. Our Ministry will be updated with your new address after that.
If you are a foreigner and would like us to update your address, please submit your supporting document, such as a phone or a utility bill printed with your name and new address through go.gov.sg/contact-bb.
Please also inform the Child Development Account (CDA) bank separately to update your address.

questions.title: I have changed my name/child's name. Do I need to inform the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) and my Child Development Account (CDA) bank?
questions.text:
If you or your child have changed name, please submit a copy of the Deed Poll or Certificate of Extract from the Registry of Births to go.gov.sg/contact-bb. We will update the name in our records.
You should also update the CDA bank separately by bringing the original Deed Poll or Certificate of Extract from the Registry of Births to any CDA bank branch.

questions.title: Will the MEP ensure I get all the maintenance that is owed to me?
questions.text:
(If you are owed maintenance)
The MEP helps to improve enforcement outcomes, but it does not guarantee full recovery in every case. Outcomes depend on the respondent’s actual financial circumstances. The aim is to achieve realistic and sustainable arrangements, especially for ongoing support needs.

questions.title: Why is the process asking for more information from me?
questions.text: Applicants are expected to provide clear information on arrears and outstanding amounts, and in appropriate circumstances, income and assets as well as other relevant information. This helps ensure that the process is based on accurate facts and allows for fair and effective outcomes.

questions.title: What role do Maintenance Enforcement Officers (MEOs) play in my case?
questions.text:
MEOs help to:
Gather relevant financial information
Facilitate discussions between parties
Support the process towards fair outcomes
They are not there to take sides, but to support a fair and informed process.

questions.title: Will the MEO take action on my behalf?
questions.text:
MEOs do not act as your representative or advocate. Instead, they help ensure that the process is:
Based on accurate information
Conducted fairly
The Court remains responsible for making decisions and recording orders.

questions.title: Why does the process include conciliation or discussions?
questions.text: Conciliation is part of the process to help parties reach practical and lasting solutions, where possible. This can sometimes lead to faster and more sustainable outcomes than relying solely on enforcement measures.

questions.title: Is the MEP just a more complicated process than before?
questions.text:
The MEP introduces new steps to address past challenges such as:
Lack of reliable financial information
Difficulty enforcing maintenance effectively
These changes are intended to improve fairness and outcomes over time.

questions.title: Is the MEP just about enforcing payment against me?
questions.text:
(If an application has been filed against you for breach of a maintenance order)
No. The MEP is not purely punitive. It is designed to achieve fair and sustainable outcomes, taking into account your actual financial situation.

questions.title: Will the MEO decide whether I am at fault or how much I should pay?
questions.text: No. MEOs do not make decisions like judges. They support the process, but the Court remains responsible for making final decisions and orders.

questions.title: Why do I need to provide financial information?
questions.text:
Providing financial information is essential to ensure that:
Your actual ability to pay is accurately understood
Any orders made are fair and proportionate

questions.title: Is the process intrusive or unfair in requesting my financial details?
questions.text: Information requests are made to support fair and informed decision-making. They allow the Court to make orders that are appropriate to your circumstances, rather than assumptions about your income or assets.

questions.title: What happens if I do not cooperate with the process?
questions.text: All parties are expected to cooperate fully, including providing requested financial information. Non-cooperation may affect how the case is assessed and the outcomes that follow (including adverse inferences drawn by the Court).

questions.title: Can the MEP help me reach a manageable arrangement?
questions.text: Yes. The process includes conciliation, where possible, to help parties reach arrangements that are realistic and sustainable given your circumstances.

questions.title: I have filed a variation application. Why do I still need to participate in the MEP?
questions.text: Until the court order that is the subject matter of the enforcement application is varied, the order remains enforceable. However, you may raise the reasons why you are seeking a variation during the conciliation session or at the enforcement hearing.

questions.title: How do I derive my MediSave contributions amount as a self-employed person?
questions.text:
Your MediSave contributions are computed based on your age and net trade income1 for the year.
You can use the Self-Employed MediSave Contribution Calculator to calculate the amount of MediSave you need to contribute.

questions.title: How do I make payment?
questions.text:
Payment is required upon registration. You can pay by:
NETS
Medisave (up to $300 per patient per year)
Major credit cards
If your payment is covered by your company or another payment scheme, please provide a Letter of Guarantee (LOG) and any supporting documents during registration.

questions.title: Do I need to apply for the MediSave Grant for Newborns for my child?
questions.text:
All eligible newborns will receive the MediSave Grant for Newborns automatically within a week from the registration of birth1, or from the date when Singapore Citizenship was granted2. You will receive a notification letter after the grant has been deposited and may check your child's CPF statement online by logging in with your Singpass at cpf.gov.sg/childdashboard.
If your child is born overseas, you can register his or her birth with the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority directly, or through the relevant Overseas Missions.
If your child is eligible for the grant but has not received it within one week of their birth registration, please write to the Central Provident Fund Board at cpf.gov.sg/writetous.
1 If your child is a Singapore Citizen at birth.
2 If your child is a Singapore Citizen by registration.

questions.title: Should I inform my employees when making Voluntary Contributions (VC) for them?
questions.text: Yes, please keep your employees informed about any Voluntary Contributions (VC) you intend to make. This will help your employees take into account any VC you make for them, if they are also making VC for themselves.
topics: Employer - Making Voluntary CPF Contributions / Voluntary contributions

questions.title: What should I do if I receive a visit pass expiry reminder after applying for a Right of Entry (ROE)?
questions.text: Please submit an enquiry via the feedback form so we can check your conversion status.

questions.title: Can I apply for Singapore citizenship confirmation for a deceased person?
questions.text: Singapore citizenship confirmation cannot be applied for on behalf of a deceased person. Citizenship status cannot be confirmed or amended after death.

questions.title: I am due to take my Oath of Renunciation, Allegiance and Loyalty (ORAL) at age 21. Can I apply for Singapore citizenship confirmation?
questions.text: Please submit an enquiry via the feedback form before applying for Singapore citizenship confirmation.

questions.title: How can I show prove that my Re-Entry Permit (REP) is linked to my passport?
questions.text: You can view your REP details, including your passport number, by logging in to MyICA with Singpass. Go to 'My Transactions' and select 'Re-Entry Permit'.
topics: PR and Re-Entry Permit Related Matters

questions.title: Why is MediShield Life applying a differentiated pro-ration factor for ward charges and surgical fees?
questions.text: As ward charges and surgical fees can differ, having a single pro-ration factor could result in over- or under-proration of individual bills. Having a differentiated pro-ration factor will allow private and unsubsidised bills to be better normalise to the subsidised equivalent.

questions.title: I was admitted to a Class A/B1 ward. Why are the pro-ration factors lowered from 1 April 2025 and how will this affect my MediShield Life claim?
questions.text:
As private hospital bills and Class A/B1 bills in public hospitals are generally higher than the Class B2/C bills that MediShield Life is designed for, they are pro-rated or normalised to the equivalent level of a Class B2/C bill before MediShield Life payouts are computed to ensure payouts are comparable.
With private and unsubsidised bills growing faster than subsidised bills, the pro-ration factors have been reduced to ensure MediShield Life payouts are comparable across different settings and to reduce cross-subsidisation .
Patients who seek private or unsubsidised care should now see comparable payouts to subsidised patients.

questions.title: My ex-spouse and I plan to sell our matrimonial property and split the sale proceeds. What should we know about CPF refunds before applying for a court order?
questions.text:
In general, the amount members must refund is the principal they have withdrawn for the property (P) and the accrued interest (I), i.e. the “P+I”. If members are age 55 or above and have pledged the property to set aside their retirement sum, they must also refund the pledged amount.
Before finalising the court order, both of you should check how much each party needs to refund to their own CPF account when the property is sold, so that they can better determine how the sale proceeds may be shared.
To check the exact amount that you need to refund your CPF accounts if you sell your property, simply log in to your Home ownership dashboard and look under the “What Happens If” section.
Important note: Scenario where members are required to refund less than their P+I
However, the required CPF refund can be less than P+I if members are:
age 55 or older before 1 January 2013; and
have set aside their Full Retirement Sum (FRS) before 1 January 2013.
This is because having set aside their FRS before 1 January 2013, members are not required by law to refund the CPF savings they used to pay for their property prior to 2013. If they continued to use their CPF savings from 1 January 2013, only the principal amount used from 1 January 2013 and the accrued interest need to be refunded when they sell their property.
Example: How much needs to be refunded?
The table below shows an example of how the required refund may be calculated.
Housing usage and Pledged amount
Amount
a. P+I before 1 January 2013
$20,000
b. P+I after 1 January 2013
$30,000
c. Pledged amount
$10,000
Required refund upon disposal:
If member set aside FRS before 1 January 2013
$40,000
[b+c]
If member did not set aside FRS before 1 January 2013
$60,000 [a+b+c]
Please note that there are some scenarios that do not require a refund to the member:
the member withdrew their CPF monies upon renouncing their Singapore citizenship or Permanent Residency; or
the member had passed away.
Differences in refund obligations between you and your ex-spouse can affect how the net sale proceeds are ultimately distributed. For example, both parties may intend to split the net sale proceeds equally after the housing loan and CPF refunds are paid. But if one party needs to make a lower CPF refund, or no refund at all, the final amounts each party receives in cash and CPF may be different. Parties should also take into account any voluntary housing refunds made, as this reduced their refund obligation and could affect the distribution of the proceeds.
You should seek legal advice so that the court order properly takes the CPF refund amounts into account and the matrimonial assets (including the sale proceeds) can be divided in an equitable manner.
topics: Other Schemes / Division of CPF-related assets in a divorce

questions.title: What is the Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals (CDRT)?
questions.text:
The CDRT is a specialised tribunal established under the State Courts of Singapore to hear cases involving intractable neighbour disputes. It acts as a court of last resort for neighbours who have failed to resolve conflicts through other means such as mediation.
For more information, you may refer to https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/community-neighbour-dispute-claims
topics: Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals / General Overview

questions.title: Who is legally considered a "neighbour" for a Community Disputes Resolution Tribunal (CDRT) claim?
questions.text:
A "neighbour" is defined as someone who lives in the same building as you or lives within a 100-meter radius of your place of residence. This excludes people living in the same household or subdivided units.
For more information, you may refer to https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/cases-eligible-neighbour-dispute-claim
topics: Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals / General Overview

questions.title: What is "unreasonable interference" under the Community Disputes Resolution Act 2015 (“the CDRA”)?
questions.text:
It refers to an act or omission by a neighbour that significantly disturbs your enjoyment or use of your home. Examples include but are not limited to excessive noise, smell, smoke, or physical obstruction of common spaces.
For more information, you may refer to https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/cases-eligible-neighbour-dispute-claim
topics: Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals / General Overview

questions.title: Is excessive noise from an upstairs neighbour a valid ground for a claim to be filed in the Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals?
questions.text:
Yes, this is one example of an act that can come under the CDRA. However, the Claimant bears the legal burden of proving on a balance of probabilities that the noise originated from the upstairs neighbour and that it is excessive.
For more information, you may refer to https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/cases-eligible-neighbour-dispute-claim
topics: Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals / General Overview

questions.title: Can I file a claim in the Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals against a neighbour for excessive second-hand smoke?
questions.text:
Yes, this is one example of an act that can come under the CDRA. However, the Claimant bears the legal burden of proving on a balance of probabilities that the cigarette smoke originated from the neighbour and that it is excessive.
For more information, you may refer to https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/cases-eligible-neighbour-dispute-claim and https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/before-making-an-application-protection-from-harassment
topics: Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals / General Overview

questions.title: What is the maximum monetary claim for damages I can make before the Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals (CDRT)?
questions.text:
The CDRT can award monetary damages of up to $20,000. If your claim for damages exceeds this amount, you may need to pursue it through the Civil Courts.
For more information, you may refer to https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/cases-eligible-neighbour-dispute-claim
topics: Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals / General Overview

questions.title: What is the time limit for filing a neighbour dispute claim in the Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals?
questions.text:
You must file your claim within 2 years from the date the episodes of unreasonable interference occurred. Claims filed after this period may be dismissed for being out of time.
For more information, you may refer to https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/how-to-file-serve-neighbour-dispute-claim
topics: Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals / General Overview

questions.title: Can I sue a government agency at the Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals?
questions.text:
No, the CDRT only hears disputes between neighbours. Claims against public authorities or government agencies generally cannot be filed before the CDRT.
For more information, you may refer to https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/cases-eligible-neighbour-dispute-claim
topics: Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals / General Overview

questions.title: Is attending mediation mandatory before filing a Community Disputes Resolution Tribinals claim?
questions.text:
As at 1 June 2026, mediation is not mandatory but strongly encouraged. However, Parliament has passed legislation to introduce mandatory pre-filing mediation, and this requirement will take effect in due course.
For more information, you may refer to https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/file-neighbour-dispute-claim
topics: Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals / Filing Process

questions.title: What is the "Pre-filing Assessment" in the Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals?
questions.text:
Before filing, you must complete an Online assessment on the CJTS portal to determine if your case is suitable for proceedings before the CDRT. You will receive a Pre-filing Assessment ID for this purpose.
For more information, you may refer to https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/how-to-file-serve-neighbour-dispute-claim
topics: Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals / Filing Process

questions.title: How much is the filing fee for a Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals claim?
questions.text:
The standard filing fee for commencing a Claim in the CDRT is S$150. Additional fees may apply for other accompanying applications or if the matter requires more than one full day of trial.
For more information, you may refer to https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/how-to-file-serve-neighbour-dispute-claim
topics: Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals / Filing Process

questions.title: Where/how do I file a Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals Claim?
questions.text:
All claims must be filed online through the Community Justice and Tribunals System (CJTS). You will need your Singpass to log in, prepare, and submit the necessary forms.
For more information, you may refer to https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/how-to-file-serve-neighbour-dispute-claim
topics: Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals / Filing Process

questions.title: What happens after I file a Community Disputes Resolution Tribunal claim?
questions.text:
After filing, you must serve the Claim documents and the Notice of Case Conference on the Respondent (the intended party to the Claim) within 14 days so the relevant neighbour is legally notified of the proceedings.
For more information, you may refer to https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/how-to-file-serve-neighbour-dispute-claim
topics: Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals / Filing Process

questions.title: How do I "serve" documents to my neighbour?
questions.text:
You should carry out service by registered post to their last known address. You must then file a Declaration of Service (DOS) on CJTS.
For more information, you may refer to https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/how-to-file-serve-neighbour-dispute-claim
topics: Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals / Filing Process

questions.title: Can I use CCTV footage as evidence in my Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals matter?
questions.text:
Yes, CCTV footage is a common form of evidence in the CDRT. You must ensure that the footage is timestamped and specifically shows the act of unreasonable interference.
For more information, you may refer to https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/prepare-evidence-neighbour-dispute-claim
topics: Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals / Filing Process

questions.title: What other types of evidence should I prepare for my Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals matter?
questions.text:
Examples of useful evidence includes but is not limited to timestamped photographs, audio/video recordings, police reports, medical reports, and logs of the dates/times the unreasonable interference occurred.
For more information, you may refer to https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/prepare-evidence-neighbour-dispute-claim
topics: Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals / Filing Process

questions.title: Are lawyers allowed in Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals proceedings?
questions.text:
Generally, lawyers are not allowed to represent parties in the CDRT unless all parties agree and the court grants permission. This keeps the process simple and affordable.
For more information, you may refer to https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/file-neighbour-dispute-claim
topics: Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals / Filing Process

questions.title: What is a Case Conference (CC)?
questions.text:
For Community Disputes Resolution Tribunal (CDRT) matters, a Case Conference is a session where a Deputy Registrar (also a judge) manages the case, conducts mediation, and sets a timeline for the trial to take place if a settlement cannot be reached.
For more information, you may refer to https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/at-neighbour-dispute-claim-pretrial-case-conference
topics: Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals / Filing Process

questions.title: What if the Respondent ignores the CDRT court notice?
questions.text:
If the Respondent fails to attend the Case Conference or trial, the judge may proceed to hear the case in the Respondent’s absence and issue a "Default Order" in your favour.
For more information, you may refer to https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/understand-outcomes-neighbour-dispute-claim
topics: Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals / Court Outcomes

questions.title: Can the CDRT order my neighbour to apologize?
questions.text:
Yes, the tribunal has the power to order the Respondent to apologise upon successful proof of the Claim.
For more information, you may refer to https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/understand-outcomes-neighbour-dispute-claim
topics: Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals / Court Outcomes

questions.title: For CDRT matters, what is an “Injunction”?
questions.text:
An injunction is a court order that requires a neighbor to stop doing something either temporarily for a specified period of time or permanently. For example, the tribunal can issue an injunction ordering a neighbour to stop playing loud music after 11 PM or to stop disposing of rubbish in the common corridor.
For more information, you may refer to https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/understand-outcomes-neighbour-dispute-claim
topics: Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals / Court Outcomes

questions.title: For CDRT matters, what is "Specific Performance"?
questions.text:
An order for specific performance is a court order that requires a neighbour to do something or to start doing something. For example, the tribunal can issue an order for specific performance requiring an individual to remove a permanent structure that has been proven to be illegally built on his neighbour's land or requiring an individual to repair a water leak that has been shown to cause flooding in his neighbour's unit.
For more information, you may refer to https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/understand-outcomes-neighbour-dispute-claim
topics: Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals / Court Outcomes

questions.title: Can I recover out-of-pocket expenses (i.e. disbursements) that I have incurred while pursuing my claim?
questions.text:
You may claim for out-of-pocket expenses incurred from the other party if you succeed in your claim. Such fees include filing fees that you have incurred. You may however be expected to prove the amount of money that you have paid and that such expenses are necessarily incurred before an order for payment of disbursements is made.
For more information, you may refer to https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/understand-outcomes-neighbour-dispute-claim
topics: Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals / Court Outcomes

questions.title: What should I do if my neighbour breaches a CDRT order?
questions.text:
If your neighbour breaches a CDRT order, you may apply for a special direction and a compliance bond (where appropriate). Before you apply, you should consider whether the other party has failed to comply with the terms of the CDRT order made against them by looking carefully at the order you have obtained. If you think they have failed to comply with the CDRT order, you will need to prepare and file evidence to support your case and application.
For more information, you may refer to https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/understand-outcomes-neighbour-dispute-claim

questions.title: What is a "Special Direction"?
questions.text:
A special direction is a direction by the CDRT to a party to comply with the order that has been made against them. Failure to comply with a special direction without a reasonable excuse is a criminal offence and the contravening party may be liable on conviction to a fine or imprisonment, or both.
For more information, you may refer to https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/apply-special-direction

questions.title: What is an "Exclusion Order"?
questions.text:
An exclusion order is an order made by the CDRT for the contravening party to be kept out of their place of residence for a specified period of time. It is used as a last resort in extreme cases of persistent nuisance. You can only apply for an exclusion order if the contravening party has failed to comply with a special direction made against them.
For more information, you may refer to https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/apply-exclusion-order
topics: Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals / Court Outcomes

questions.title: Can I appeal against an order made by the Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals?
questions.text:
Yes, but you must first apply for "leave" (or permission) to appeal within 14 days after the order is issued. If leave is granted, the appeal is heard by the General Division of the High Court.
For more information, you may refer to https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/appeal-against-neighbour-dispute-claim-order-tribunal

questions.title: How do I set aside a default order made by the CDRT in my absence?
questions.text:
If a default order was made against you because you failed to attend the Case Conference or trial and if you wish to challenge this order, you must file an application to set aside the default order and explain why you were absent (including providing the necessary documentation to substantiate your reason(s)).
For more information, you may refer to https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/set-aside-neighbour-dispute-claim-order-made-in-absence
topics: Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals / Court Outcomes

questions.title: Does the CDRT handle inter-floor water leakage?
questions.text:
The CDRT can adjudicate such matters if the water leakage is alleged to be the consequence of an act or omission that is an unreasonable interference in breach of the CDRA. The remedies that you can seek for water leakage from the CDRT is however limited to those available under the CDRA. You may wish to consider seeking legal advice on whether it is more appropriate for you to file a claim in the civil courts.
For more information, you may refer to https://www.judiciary.gov.sg/civil/cases-eligible-neighbour-dispute-claim
topics: Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals / General Overview

questions.title: Can a landlord be held liable for a tenant's behaviour?
questions.text:
